subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that negotiations between Canada and the United States for the co-operative development of the water resources of the Columbia river system are to commence in Ottawa on Thursday, February 11.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) will be the chairman of the Canadian delegation, other members being Mr. Robertson, deputy minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources; Mr. A. E. Ritchie, assistant undersecretary, Department of External Affairs and Mr. E. W. Bassett, deputy minister of lands and forests of the province of British Columbia.
The United States delegation will have as its chairman Mr. E. F. Bennett, undersecretary, department of interior, other members being Mr. I. B. White, assistant secretary, department of state, and Lieutenant General E. C. Itschner, chief, United States army corps of engineers.
An announcement similar to the one given by me will be made simultaneously in the United States.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is of such great importance to British Columbia and to the people of Canada generally that I cannot resist making a few remarks in regard to the Prime Minister's statement.
The Prime Minister's important announcement indicates that Canada is ready to make her contribution to the energy needs of British Columbia and the Pacific northwest. All power development has a price but, under the right conditions, this can provide a bargain for the people on both sides of the international boundary. The Prime Minister's announcement shows clearly that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) and his colleagues have worked successfully in this direction in a spirit of equity and justice for all governments and peoples concerned. It is doubtful, in my opinion and in the opinion of a good many others, whether anything in recent times affecting the national interests of Canada and the United States will prove of much greater importance in 79951-0-17
the years to come than agreement reached by the governments of Canada and the United States on the equitable and scientific development of the Columbia river.
We congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs on his skilful and persistent efforts to make a long standing dream come true. I did not quite hear the Prime Minister correctly as to who was to be the chairman of the Canadian team.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING
speechtext: The Minister of Justice.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING
speechtext:
I thought so but I was not quite certain. Anyway, I might say that we are most interested in the personnel of the negotiating team for Canada. It may interest the house to know that the father of the Minister of Justice, Hon. Frederick Fulton of Kamloops, chief commissioner of lands for the province of British Columbia under Sir Richard McBride's administration, blazed a trail for the development of conservation policies in British Columbia, and was also a member of the first royal commission on conservation established by an act of this parliament.
We think it most fitting that his son, the present Minister of Justice and a native British Columbian, will head the Canadian team. We know all members of the house, regardless of party, will wish them every success for a speedy and successful conclusion of their labours.
While the Prime Minister's announcement will be received by all members in this house and the people of British Columbia with satisfaction and high hopes that the great projects envisioned for the development of the Columbia in Canada will soon commence, we trust it will also chill the enthusiasm of Mr. Main-waring and his associates for premature and less desirable developments.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with the exception of the personal observations made by the hon. gentleman, I am sure he will permit me to say that the epitome of all his remarks could not have been better made by any of us on this side of the house.

I wish to make an announcement, Mr. Speaker, respecting the fifth meeting of the joint Canada-United States committee on trade and economic affairs. This meeting will

Inquiries of the Ministry be held in Washington on February 16, and 17, the last meeting having been in Ottawa in January, 1959.
Canada will be represented by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture. subtopic: LIVESTOCK

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: LIVESTOCK
subsubtopic: ONTARIO-INFECTION OF CALVES BY NEMATODIRUS PARASITE
speechtext: I wish to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. What steps are being taken by the federal Department of Agriculture to check the spread of the new parasitic disease called nematodiriasis, which has infected calves in Ontario?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: LIVESTOCK
subsubtopic: ONTARIO-INFECTION OF CALVES BY NEMATODIRUS PARASITE
speechtext:
This is not a new disease, as the parasite nematodirus which causes the disease has been found in sheep and cattle in all parts of Canada for a considerable number of years. There is no intermediate host in the spread of this small intestinal worm, reinfection taking place directly from infected pastures. Normally, extreme cold weather destroys any eggs or larvae remaining on pastures over winter. A new drug, hepherium embronate, has been developed for use against this parasite.
This parasitic infection does not come under the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act; therefore no federal program exists for its eradication. Research workers of this department's health of animals division collaborate with veterinary workers of the provinces in identifying the parasite and in providing advice to practising veterinarians and livestock owners.
As indicated earlier, the disease is not a new one, and it is not thought to be on the increase. It is understood that the purpose of the press release from the Ontario department of agriculture was merely to draw to the attention of livestock owners and practising veterinarians that cases of scours in cattle may well be caused by this parasite.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday I had very nearly completed my remarks, and I merely wish to conclude by repeating that I congratulate the government on the appointment of the royal commission to examine into our coal problem, because of the many misunderstandings that exist concerning coal in Canada.
As I was closing on the last day I mentioned that a tariff against United States coal in itself would probably not do very much for the Nova Scotia coal industry. The most serious competitor of Nova Scotia coal is residual oil which is imported from Venezuela and, in recent months, natural gas. A tariff against Venezuelan residual oil would be of much more benefit to the Nova Scotia coal industry, particularly in our natural market of Quebec, than a tariff against United States coal. Of course an increased tariff against United States coal would in some areas be of

assistance to us, but certainly would not be as valuable as a tariff against residual oil.
I am glad to see that this very important problem of coal is being gone into, and I do hope the people of Canada will realize that coal is the energy fuel of the future; it is the long term cheap fuel, and therefore it is a wise investment for Canadians, as they are doing now in the present subvention program, to assist the movement of coal to market and to protect this resource industry for use in the development of Canada in the future.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, during the hon. member's remarks, at page 253 of Hansard, he referred to me as having suggested that the answer to some problems he had posed was for the Bank of Canada to print money. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I want to ask a question, based on remarks the hon. member made the other day in the middle of his speech. In view of the remarks he made about tight money, does he agree now that there is no tight money situation in Canada, and has not been in the last few years?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course there is a tight money situation in Canada, but not necessarily a tight money policy on the part of the government. The important thing is that, under the big demand for money in the nation today there is a high interest rate that cannot be controlled by this government or any other single borrower in the nation, because rates are set by the lender or by negotiation between the lender and the borrower and no one agency, the government or any other, can of itself alone set the interest rates in the nation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is not what the Prime Minister said in the election campaign.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall dispense with the formalities of complimenting the mover (Mr. Morissette) and the seconder (Mrs. Casselman) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne and the newly appointed ministers and parliamentary secretaries by associating myself with the compliments which our leader has already extended on our behalf.
Most speeches from the throne are described as being more notable for what they omit than what they contain. I doubt whether in the history of this parliament there has been an emptier speech from the throne than the one under debate. The beginning of a new decade seems to me an appropriate time to review the past and take stock of ourselves,

to determine our mistakes and take whatever decisions are necessary to avoid repeating them in the future.
One would have hoped, therefore, that this particular speech from the throne above all others would have told the people of Canada some sober truths; that it would have pointed out where we have gone wrong in the past as a people and a nation, and that it would have challenged and inspired us to gird our loins and go forward with faith and courage to take the necessary action to get back on the right road. For it is clear that we cannot go travelling the old road of expediency as we have done in the past, engrossed in our own selfishness, living beyond our means, building up a standard of living beyond the capacity of our economy to support, trying to establish a little island of prosperity for ourselves here in Canada with little thought or regard for the starving, poverty stricken millions in other parts of the world and in some parts of our own country. The road we have been travelling leads to destruction, and the action necessary to save ourselves involves painful and courageous decisions.
For my own province the decade just ended has been the most important in our 450 years of history. In 1949 Newfoundland made the momentous decision to give up her independent status as a British dominion and become a part of Canada. It was an act of faith, because once in there is no way to get out. We came into confederation realizing that we were putting ourselves completely at the mercy of the Canadian government. Should the government of Canada choose to place a narrow interpretation upon the terms of union, or to ignore the spirit in which they were made, we knew that we had no means of redress and would be helpless to do anything about it. Our security lay in the Canadian constitution, which we thought would never be violated, and in the honour and integrity of the Canadian people, which we believed would be a sufficient guarantee that our simple trust would be respected and that the solemn treaty between our two peoples would be fully implemented both in the letter and in the spirit.
That trust has been severely shaken by events which have taken place during the past two years, and many sincere people in my province are wondering whether it was ever justified. We must all make it our first duty and responsibility to do everything possible that this division may be healed and good faith restored, and a new spirit of unity created between us.
Our first ten years as Canadians have brought us many blessings but also many disappointments. Our cost of living, which 79951-0-18
The Address-Mr. Carter was already high before we entered confederation, went up instead of down as we had expected; Canadian capital has not been forthcoming for the development of our resources. Our system of communications, despite improvements, still leaves much to be desired. But our greatest disappointment has been that the government of Canada so far has refused to recognize the fact that, having missed for 80 years the benefits of confederation which enabled the mainland provinces to develop a relatively high standard of public services, the position of Newfoundland is therefore different from that of any other province and should be treated as a special case.
We have many deficiencies in our public services, especially those of health, roads and education. But with an economy based on primary industries and a rapidly expanding population we cannot maintain even our existing standards, let alone improve them, unless we receive special consideration. As a group, our fishermen have benefited least of all from confederation. Like the farmers, their cost of living has steadily increased year by year while the price of their product has remained the same and indeed is lower than it was during the first world war. The premium on the Canadian dollar penalizes our chief exports of fish and paper, and the freight rate structure handicaps our manufacturing industries and prevents them from competing in the mainland market.
As a result we always have the largest percentage of unemployed in all of Canada. Our total of unemployed is now as large as it was last year, which was abnormal, and the projected closing of Fort Pepperrell will make that situation even worse.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Nothing is being done about it, either.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
These are the problems which face our province as we enter the sixties. But as we look out over the nation as a whole we see even greater problems-tight money, inflation, unemployment, labour-management relations, dominion-provincial relations, wheat surpluses, defence problems and trade deficits. These formidable problems face the Canadian people as a whole, and unless we can find solutions or make reasonable progress toward solutions during the next ten years there is great danger that our economic structure may collapse.
The common factor in all these problems is the money problem. During world wars I and II we saw nations accumulate debt burdens until they collapsed. Then we saw these same countries, having got rid of their debt burdens, make an economic recovery so strong and so rapid that within a few

The Address-Mr. Carter short years they were able to compete successfully with those nations whose economies had suffered no set-back whatsoever. Germany has demonstrated this phenomenon twice in less than 50 years. On the other hand the creditor nations suffered no lasting ill effects from their failure to collect these huge debts. Then there are cases where interest charges are such that the original loan is repaid several times over and the borrower still finds himself in debt. No thinking person who ponders these facts can help feeling that there must be something wrong with a system which produces such results.
Money is a man-made device. It was invented to facilitate the exchange and distribution of the things we produce. Money was meant to be man's servant, but it has become his master. From a relatively simple concept as a medium of exchange it has become more and more complex, until today it has become a sort of Frankenstein which men can no longer control, a monster capable of exercising the power of life and death over man through its influence on employment and other economic factors upon which his livelihood and welfare depend.
To me it is significant that not a single new idea for the improvement of our monetary system has emerged during the past 100 years. It has become a sacred cow. Surely the human brain, which can make atom bombs and put man-made satellites into orbit, is capable of developing a simpler and better monetary system than we have today, one that is simple enough for the average Canadian to understand and that will at the same time satisfy our economic requirements without the disadvantages and paradoxes of our present system.
One of Canada's greatest needs today is a dollar that will remain stable, that will not penalize our exporters, that will not restrict industrial development and the utilization of resources in the underdeveloped parts of our country. Our present monetary system makes the rich richer and the poor poorer. It tends to make big corporations bigger and small firms smaller. It facilitates the development of those parts of our country where industrialization is already high and retards the development of those parts where industrial devolopment is low. It puts a premium on imports and penalizes our exports. I suggest to the government that the time has come when a royal commission or some other body representing all sections of our society should be set up to study our monetary system and make recommendations for its improvement.
Next to a stable currency Canada needs people. Our best protection against overdependence on external trade is to build up


our home market as rapidly as possible. Since the natural growth of our population cannot do this fast enough we shall have to abandon the rather cautious and selfish immigration policy which we now pursue. We need people so desperately to expand our domestic market that we can no longer afford to insist on bringing them in at our own convenience and pleasure, and in such limited numbers.
Those who fear that the immigrant may put a Canadian out of a job should bear in mind that if that immigrant does not come to Canada some Canadian will lose his job anyway. Large scale immigration may work hardships on a few Canadian, but unless it takes place all Canadians will ultimately suffer.
In the field of international trade forces are coming into existence that will make Canada's position more difficult than at any time in our history. If we do not assess these forces correctly and take the proper course of action we may very well find ourselves squeezed out of our overseas markets. Since 20 per cent of our jobs depend upon external trade, this would be fatal for the Canadian economy. We must diversify our foreign markets, but we cannot take the risk of permitting ourselves to become dependent on trade with the communist bloc. We should make a special effort to expand our trade with Japan, which promises to become an important market for our surplus wheat and coal. Japan already buys more from us than we do from her, and it is obvious that she cannot increase her purchases from Canada unless we buy more of her products.
However, as soon as we increase our imports from Japan our own industries cry out for tariff protection keep Japanese goods out. We should bear in mind that the lower priced Japanese articles benefit the Canadian consumer and leave more money in his pocket to spend on local products. This problem illustrates the conflict of interest between different groups of Canadians. The interests and welfare of Canadians in the prairie provinces are directly opposed to the interests and welfare of Canadians in central Canada who depend mainly on our manufacturing industries.
Obviously such a conflict cannot be resolved without someone getting hurt, but the problem must be tackled, and at once. This involves an agonizing reappraisal of our tariff and trade policies. It calls for courageous action, and it requires a spirit of understanding and unselfishness on the part of all Canadians so that any resulting hardship to those affected will be minimized.
In working out solutions to our domestic problems organized labour will play a key role. The fate and the future of Canada rest

more in the hands of labour than in those of any other group. This puts a heavy responsibility upon our labour leaders and demands from them the highest quality of statesmanship. But before labour can play its full part it must get back to fundamental principles. The fact must be recognized by both labour and management that every individual, whether he be a labourer or employer, has worth within himself as a created being, that he has certain God-given rights which must not be circumscribed or interfered with by the state, by management or by a union. The employer has the right to make his own decisions in accordance with his conscience in carrying out his responsibilities to the nation. The worker has the right to join the union of his choice. He has also an equal right not to join if he so desires. The right to associate is no greater than the right not to associate.
No organization, whether it be a corporation or a union, is more important than the individual. No organization can be permitted to place itself above the law of the land, and the national interest must always be paramount. Freedom is indivisible, and no individual worker or employer should be compelled to forfeit these inalienable rights or be penalized for exercising them. However, labour and management must realize also that their prime task now is to make the class war obsolete, just as obsolete as any other kind of war, and that the use of strikes in the settlement of disputes is just as outdated as the use of other forms of force. It is futile to try to settle a dispute on the basis of who is right because neither party is ever 100 per cent right.
On the other hand, there is no dispute which cannot be settled in a matter of hours, if not minutes, on the basis of what is morally right for the union and for management, both having regard to the best interests of the nation as a whole. Very often the barriers to settlement are not economic but human pride, greed, selfishness and the lust for power and prestige. Under those circumstances, no worth-while settlement can be reached without a change of heart and attitude on the part of every individual.
Granted good will and the right kind of human relationship, it should be possible for management and labour to work out agreements that would ensure that the benefits of increased productivity would be passed on to the consumer in the form of lower prices. Our dollar would then be stabilized and everybody would benefit from the increased purchasing power. Such a step would go a long way toward curing the problem of inflation, because it would reverse the forces that cause it.
79951-0-18i
The Address-Mr. Carter
While I am on the subject of labour I should like to plead with the government to give an early increase to those civil servants whose salaries are now too low to permit them to live and raise their families with the decency and dignity that befits a human being. I am sure hon. members were surprised, as I was, to learn that such a large percentage in the different categories of civil servants earn less than $300 per month, which is the very minimum upon which a family can live at today's prices.
I know the Minister of Finance is anxious to balance the budget, but the welfare of the individual and his family should be the first charge upon our economy, not for his working period only but during his retirement years as well. It has always been my experience that when we take a step in faith and do the right thing for the right motives, a way is always found to take care of the expenses incurred.
The problem of national defence changes so rapidly and has been rendered so complicated and costly by the rapid advances in technological developments that it is difficult to make any long term plans. While we must arm ourselves militarily with the best weapons our economy can afford, yet unless we also arm ourselves ideologically we cannot hope to survive. We must win the ideological battle or there can be no victory on any front. I therefore heartily concur in all the remarks concerning this topic which the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Kuche-repa) made a few days ago.
To any student of current events who has even an elementary knowledge of the forces at work in ourselves, in our nation and in the world at large, it must be apparent that the sixties may well turn out to be the most dangerous decade in our history, not only for Canada but for the whole free world. The fate of democracy and the fate of our children and succeeding generations may well, and in all probability will, be decided within the next 10 years. The question as to whether democracy will continue to endure or will disappear altogether, the question as to whether our children and their children will continue to enjoy our democratic freedoms and institutions or will become slaves of a powerful materialistic state, will quite likely be decided during the decade of the sixties. This is a fearsome thought, but it is much later than many of us care to think.
The ideological struggle between the communist world and the free world has now entered a final and decisive stage, and whether democracy will survive or perish will depend upon whether we of the free world will awake to our peril in time, and whether we will have the courage to arm

The Address-Mr. Carter ourselves with an ideology that is superior to communism. Such an ideology does exist and is available. It has been developed in the moral rearmament centres at Mackinac island in the United States and at Caux in Switzerland. Its superiority over communism has been demonstrated over and over again. For a hard, realistic assessment of this ideology, what better authority could we have than the communists themselves? This is the appraisal that was given by radio Moscow itself in January, 1953:
Moral rearmament Is a global ideology with bridgeheads in every nation in its final phase of total expansion throughout the world. It has the power to capture radical revolutionary minds. It is contaminating the minds of the masses. It substitutes for the class war, the eternal struggle between good and evil.
The constant attacks now emanating from communist sources is evidence that this ideology is the one thing about the free world the communist leaders really fear. For us who live in the free world the question is, do we have the courage to embrace this ideology and arm ourselves with it? Here is an opportunity for Canada to lead the world. Are Canadians prepared and willing to give that leadership? Unless we of the free world make this decision soon we have no chance of winning the ideological battle, and our democratic freedoms and institutions as we know them will die. Mr. Khrushchev was not joking when he said, "We will bury you."
Peaceful coexistence is a beautiful theory and very attractive to those who do not wish to face reality. Let us not be deceived by it. Mr. Khrushchev has been extremely frank about what he means by coexistence. This is what he said in a statement following the Geneva conference in 1955:
Certain people misunderstand the Geneva spirit. They ought to remember, once and for all, that we never renounce, and never will renounce, our ideas, our struggle for the victory of communism. There will never be such a thing as our ideological disarmament.
Later in the same year he said, and I quote from the New York Herald-Tribune of September 18, 1955:
Russia's smiles are sincere, but this does not change our conviction that communism will triumph throughout the world.
We will win, but we will not have to go to war about It.
They say in the west that something has changed since the Geneva conference. They say that the Soviet leaders smile, but that their actions do not match their smiles. But the smiles are sincere. They are not artificial. We wish to live in peace. But if anyone thinks that our smiles mean that we abandon the teachings of Marx and Lenin or abandon our communist road, then they are fooling themselves.
We are for coexistence. But we are also for the growth of communism. The only reason we are for coexistence is that in actual fact we are confronted

with the reality of two different systems. You capitalists go your way, so long as you do not see that it is the way of the blind.
Victory for socialism? We don't have to go to war to obtain this victory. Peaceful competition will be enough.
What language could be plainer or more unequivocal? During the past four years Mr. Khrushchev has repeatedly made statements which made clear beyond any shadow of doubt that during this period of so-called peaceful co-existence the ideological struggle will continue unabated, and will be pursued with all means short of a shooting war until the victory of communism is complete.
During the past two years we have seen the communists gain a foothold in the Caribbean, right in our own backyard. It was done so quietly and unobstrusively that some of us do not yet realize what has happened. Certainly we have not shown any particular concern about it, apart from the academic question as to whether Premier Castro is or is not a communist.
That question is completely beside the point. The facts are that the control of the Cuban economy is now in the hands of Ernesto Che Guevara, a trained communist. The armed forces are under the command of Raul C. Castro, Fidel's brother, who was trained as a communist in Prague. The land reform institute, (INRA) is being run by three well known communists, namely Antonio Nunez Jiminez, Waldo Medina Mendez and Oscar Pino Santas.
The point is therefore that regardless of whether Premier Castro is a communist, the control of Cuba is now completely in communist hands, and they are consolidating it as a beachhead for the ideological invasion of Latin America. We must never forget that the victory of communism means the death of democracy. Coexistence leads to nonexistence.
So anxious is Mr. Khrushchev to sell us this idea of peaceful coexistence that his propaganda machine is working overtime trying to frighten us into thinking that we must choose between coexistence and war. These, of course, are false alternatives. There is another alternative. I should like to quote the words of Mr. R. Vaitheswaran, a lecturer in economics at Hyderabad university, India, a man so brilliant that he recently placed first among 23,000 candidates in the Indian administrative service examination. Speaking to an assembly in July of last year Mr. Vaitheswaran had this to say:
In the communist dictionary "coexistence" means take-over by every method short of a shooting war.
How can there be coexistence when the communists have decided to fight until they rule the world? Communism would not be communism if it were not a fight to the bitter end.

By "coexistence" Khrushchev means that Russia retains the right to rule unrestrictedly in her own sphere. He also means freedom for Russia to spread her own ideological poison through her state-subsidized theatre and propaganda and to engineer internal revolutions and crises through the communist parties of the world.
The communist party in every country is a united force fighting for a single world revolution.
Coexistence gives the Soviet the right to infiltrate the democracies without the democratic countries having the right to say what they like about Soviet behaviour.
Russia goes unchallenged when she publicizes on every continent the racial division of Little Rock and the decadence of Hollywood. But America is met by strong opposition when she expresses sympathy for the captive nations.
China is free to destroy Tibet, but America is not free to rescue Hungary.
And the most shocking thing of all is not that China and Russia are what they are, but that we have become what the Russians and Chinese would like us to be-their willing tools for our own destruction.
Moral rearmament is democracy's true ideology. It gives democracy the moral fibre it lacks today. That is why the choice for the world is not war or coexistence. It is moral rearmament or communism.
These words coming from a man who spent six years as a member of the communist party and who spent two and one-half years in jail for his convictions should carry great significance.
As we turn to the international scene we see still more formidable problems which affect the peace and security of the world, and for which solutions must be found during the decade we have now begun.
Most of the problems that we face, at home and abroad, are manmade. They are the result of our moral failures, and can only be solved by finding the answer to the human fears, hate, greed and selfishness that caused them. Such solutions are beyond human wisdom and cleverness. No legislation, no political manoeuvres, no party platform can provide the answer. They can be solved only through a change of heart in the people concerned.
Fortunately there is hope because, as we look back over the past decade, we can see many instances where this kind of miracle has taken place. A few years ago there were in Cyprus, in Lebanon, and in the Far East problems which seemed incapable of solution. They were examples of the irresistible force meeting the immovable object. Yet through a change of heart in certain people good relations have now been restored between Japan and the Philippines and between Japan and Formosa and Korea. The crises in the Middle East have subsided. The shooting has stopped in Cyprus, and great progress is being made toward finding a solution to that problem in spite of communist efforts to prevent it. These miracles of change in the human heart point
The Address-Mr. Harkness the way whereby solutions can be found to the Palestinian refugee problem and the problems of Algeria and Berlin.
If there is one lesson we Canadians should have learned from our experience in the fifties it is that we cannot have our cake and eat it too. We have persisted far too long in trying to do this. The day of reckoning has now caught up with us, and it seems to me that the speech from the throne missed an excellent opportunity to sound a clarion call to the people of Canada to take stock of ourselves, to assess our shortcomings and make up our minds to correct them, no matter how painful the consequences.
During this decade many young people will grow up and participate in the affairs of our nation. What better challenge can we hold out to the youth of our country than that they not only build strong and vigorous bodies but that they keep themselves clean, tough and strong mentally and morally as well. The strength of a nation lies in the character of her people. As I am, so is my nation.
Should a war break out today many of these young people would rush to offer their lives for their country, as their fathers have done before them. We hope the day will never come when young Canadians will again have to die for their country. But Canada today needs her people to live for her-really to live-selfless lives dedicated to making their country morally strong. This can often be more difficult than dying for one's country. There is a hunger for great living in every human heart. All mankind is longing for a world that will be free from fear and hate and greed. The only way to that kind of world is along the road of absolute moral standards and divine guidance. That means moral change for every single one of us, and that kind of change can be both painful and costly. However, our survival as a free people depends upon it. Unless we are prepared to pay that price, democracy as we know it will perish.
In a time of great danger Sir Winston Churchill could offer his people nothing but blood, sweat and tears, and they rallied and responded magnificently. Today our danger is not so apparent but it is no less real. There is still time for us to repair the deficiencies in the speech from the throne. The needs of the hour demand moral leadership. If we have the courage to give it, Mr. Speaker, we need not worry about the Canadian people accepting it.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to compliment the mover (Mr. Morissette) and the seconder (Mrs. Oasselman) of the address in

The Address-Mr. Harkness reply to the speech from the throne on the excellent speeches they made. I should particularly like to say how delighted I was at the very fine speech made by the seconder, as she is an old friend of mine. I have known not only her but her late husband and her father and have been very close friends with them over many years.
I should like to take advantage of the opportunity this debate provides in order to say something about our agricultural program and problems, and also to reply to the remarks on this subject made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).
This distinguished hon. member of our house created something of a record, I believe, for speeches on agriculture on January 18, in that he was successful in making hardly one valid remark or using one correct statistic except when he was quoting directly from something I had said, or from the "Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada" for November, 1959. Unfortunately, while he gave the impression that he was quoting from this last mentioned publication, at times he was actually using the figures in a different way from which they appeared in that publication.
I might also say that the Leader of the Opposition accomplished this considerable feat in spite of the fact that his remarks on agriculture take up more than three full pages of Hansard. It is, I think, a remarkably good illustration of the truth of the old saying, "If you don't know what you are talking about, it is much wiser to keep quiet".
However, Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of sympathy for the Leader of the Opposition in the situation in which he finds himself, for neither he nor any of his followers in the house have the knowledge, background or experience in agricultural matters to enable them to speak with correctness or authority on agriculture.
Of course that is nonsense.

The chief spokesman, of course, is the distinguished lawyer from Essex East, and I do not think many farmers in this country will pay much attention to his expertness or give him much credence when he speaks on agricultural matters.
Will the minister deny that I know more than he does about agriculture?
Oh, oh.
Mr. Speaker, the laughter in the house indicates the answer.
The laughter on that side.

However, in these circumstances the opposition have to fumble and bumble along as best they can, and I can only hope that they will learn more quickly in the future than apparently they have in the past. The Leader of the Opposition started to quote from a speech I made here on January 23, 1959, and his remarks appear on page 55 of Hansard for January 18, 1960. He quotes me as saying:
-the cost-price squeeze has been finally halted.
Then he proceeded to try to pour all sorts of ridicule and scorn on that statement in order to attempt to establish that it was incorrect.
That is the minister's statement of January 23, 1959?
That is correct.
That statement of the minister was absolutely incorrect.
Mr. Speaker, may I request the exuberant hon. member for Essex East to let me make my speech.
That is right; I am sorry.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The minister interrupts
everybody else.

I must ask the hon. member not to constantly interrupt me as he has done; he has much more on Hansard to date than I. I would also request that the time taken up be not subtracted from the 40 minutes I am allowed.
The Leader of the Opposition, as I was saying, quoted this statement of mine and attempted to establish that it was incorrect; and, I might say, jumped forward a year in his quotations and statistics in an effort to do so. 1 would like to indicate what the situation was when I spoke here a year ago, in order to show that the statistics bear out that statement absolutely.
The farm cash income in Canada during 1957 was $2,577.3 million, compared to $2,847 million in 1958, an increase of $269.7 million or 10.5 per cent over 1957. The Canadian index of prices of goods and services which the farmers had to buy in 1957-this is exclusive of living costs; it is the index of goods and services farmers had to buy- was 255.9 and 259.9 in 1958, an increase of 1.6 per cent over 1957. Also, farm net income in 1957 was $1,061.5 million compared to $1,277.6 million in 1958, an increase of $216.1 million or 20.4 per cent over 1957.
I think these figures show conclusively that the farm income went up very much more in 1958 than farm costs did; and, of course, I think it is apparent this means that the cost-price squeeze was not operating.

The income farmers received was up a great deal more than the costs of the goods and services they had to buy, so that the cost-price squeeze a year ago, as I stated during
1958,	had been halted. There is no question about that if anyone understands what the cost-price squeeze really is.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring the matter up to date and quote the figures as far as we have them for 1959, just to show what the situation is now. We have the figures so far for farm income and for cost of services, and so on, that the farmer had to buy, for the first nine months; I expect that the figures for the whole year will be available within the next two weeks. However, I want it to be borne in mind that I am speaking only of the statistics for the first nine months. The figures show that the farm cash income for the first nine months of 1958 was $2,007.8 million, compared to $2,048.4 million during the same period of 1959, an increase of $40.7 million or 2 per cent over the first nine months of 1958. The index of prices of goods and services which the farmers had to buy in 1958 was 259.9 compared to 267.9 in 1959, an increase of 3.1 per cent.
In other words, during 1959-and I do not attempt to conceal the fact-the cost of goods and services which farmers had to buy went up more rapidly than their income; therefore you could say that the cost-price squeeze was operating again to a slight extent during
1959.	But as I say, unlike some of the hon. members opposite I do not try to conceal or misinterpret any of the statistics; I put them forward as they appear, and I take considerable objection to hon. members opposite, particularly the Leader of the Opposition, attempting to use partial statistics and full statistics to create a completely incorrect impression.
This is not the full story, however. I would like to go on and indicate what the situation is in 1959 over what it was in 1957 when hon. members opposite were on the treasury benches, to show that a very considerable improvement has taken place. Farm cash income for the first nine months of 1957 was $1,845.9 million and $2,048.4 million during the same period in 1959, an increase of $202.5 million or 11 per cent over the first nine months of 1957. The index of prices of goods and services which farmers had to buy was 255.9 in 1957 and 267.9 in 1959, an increase of 4.7 per cent over 1957. These figures, Mr. Speaker, I think make it abundantly clear that over this two-year period the rise in income was well over twice as great as the rise in costs.
I do not pretend that the rate of improvement in 1958 was maintained in 1959, but I
The Address-Mr. Harkness do maintain-and the statistics show this- that the situation is much better now than it was when the Liberal party were in office two and one half years ago. Also during this two-year period, farmers' income went up more than twice as much as the cost of the goods and services they had to buy.
Why does not the minister take a ten-year period, not one?

The Leader of the Opposition then attempted to show that there was a disparity between my remarks at the dominion-provincial economic conference in November, 1959 and the agriculture department's publication "Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada" put out at the same time. I quote again from page 55 of Hansard, where the Leader of the Opposition quoted me as saying:
Agricultural industry shared in the economic recovery that began in 1958 and continued into 1959.
Then he went on to say that this was completely at variance with what the department's review stated, and he quoted from that review:
In 1959, realized farm net income is expected to remain close to the 1958 level.
Well, the figures I have just given show that there is no disparity whatever between those two statements. I said that agriculture in general shared in the economic recovery that began in 1958 and continued in 1959. It did share in that recovery. The net income went up 20 per cent in 1958 as compared with 1957. The cash income went up over 10 per cent. Certainly agriculture shared in the economic recovery. That is not in any way at variance with the statement made in the review put out at the end of last year that realized farm net income in 1959 was expected to be close to that of 1958. I know the Leader of the Opposition can read English and can understand it. I find it difficult, therefore, to understand why he should try to make the case that two statements of this sort are at variance with each other, for it is clear that there is no disparity between them whatsoever.
Following that the Leader of the Opposition went on positively to gloat over the statement made in the review-a statement which I made myself, and which is to be found at page 56-to the effect that farm net income in 1960 will likely be lower than in 1959.
As I said, I do not attempt to conceal the true facts from the farmers of Canada, as some people do. I put them in the picture as far as I know it and can see it, and we in the department think that this will be the situation, and for very good reasons. First of all, the early snowstorm in the west will mean

The Address-Mr. Harkness that a certain amount of grain will be lost and that a considerable amount more will be poorer in quality, with a resulting lower price. That is one factor which will mean that the income of farmers will likely be lower in 1960 than in 1959, because they will be selling that grain in 1960. In addition, this year we expect, as a result of the policies we put into effect with respect to hogs and eggs, that marketing of hogs and eggs will be less extensive. This is essential if we are to get the hog and egg situation into a reasonable condition in this country; and when these two factors are taken into consideration it is easy to see why there may be some decrease in farmers' gross or cash income in 1960 as compared with 1959 and, therefore, some decrease in their net income.
However, the Leader of the Opposition went on to misunderstand me completely, and I can only say his remarks were bound to mislead anybody reading what he had to say. He did this by saying later, in the same paragraph on page 56, that I and other ministers had claimed that the farmers now enjoyed a fair share of the national income. I have never made that statement, and no other minister of this government has ever made that statement to my knowledge.
Where did that appear?

It is a complete misstatement. It begins on page 56 in the same paragraph as that in which the Leader of the Opposition said that farm net income in 1960 would likely be lower than in 1959. It is a complete misstatement, and it was never made by me or by any other minister. It was put in entirely for political purposes; an example of the general demagoguery which characterized his speech.

You said it all over the
country.

I defy hon. members opposite to produce any report of any speech in which I made that statement. We have stated, and we continue to state, that all our efforts are designed toward reaching that situation and giving the farmers of this country a fair share of the national income, but we have never said we have succeeded completely in doing that. As I say, the hon. member was attributing to us something we have never said; an example of the general inaccuracy and misinterpretation of which he was guilty in the speech to which I am referring.
As a matter of fact there was a greater attempt at misrepresentation, one which I think was quite evidently designed to enable him to crawl out from under. An obvious misstatement occurs just after this, and then there are the remarks of the Leader of the


Opposition just after the dinner recess which are to be found at page 59. I will quote the two passages and compare them in order to substantiate what I am saying.
On page 56, after the hon. member had just made this statement to which I have taken objection, I got up and said:
Is the hon. gentleman aware of the fact that farm income increased in 1958 some 20 per cent over 1954 and 1955, some 7 per cent over 1956 and 10 per cent over 1957, and that 1959 saw the highest income farmers have ever had in the history of Canada?
That was for the first nine months, of course. Then the record goes on:

I am aware of that. I am also aware of this, that while farm income increased in 1958 over 1957 and some years before by the amounts the minister indicated the farm income of that year, which he has singled out, was over $100 million less than the average of the 10-year period before that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is that another from the Martin bureau of statistics?
Does the minister deny it?

I deny it absolutely. You had better have your staff look at the figures, because they have made a terrible error.
Now we turn to page 59. During the dinner recess the minister had two hours in which to look over what he had said before- his blue sheets-and decide what he was going to say later. If he had gone right on to make the statement he made on page 59 without having had those two hours in which to consider things I would not take such objection to what he said, but having this time available, he yet came back and tried to misinterpret the facts and state something different from what he had said in the quotation I have just given the house, trying to place it on the basis of net income instead of general income or cash income. And to show that the Leader of the Opposition did not know what he was talking about in connection with these things, may I point out that the figures I quoted were farm income, cash income; they had nothing to do with net income. If the Leader of the Opposition had known what he was talking about-
Perhaps the minister would read Hansard again. He would realize that I was talking about farm net income before the recess, and I mentioned that in my statement before the recess.

All you have to do is refer to Hansard and read the sections I am quoting. As I pointed out, the figures I gave -with which the Leader of the Opposition agreed-are figures for cash income. Then, having seen during the dinner recess that he had made an obvious error, the Leader of the Opposition came back and tried to crawl out

of it by making the statement which appears on page 59. I quote from column 1:
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture was really quite vigorous in his denial of some of my statements this afternoon and took strong exception to a statement which I made that the average net farm income for the period 1946 to 1956 was over $100 million more than the net income in 1958.
If the hon. gentleman will permit me to say so, we were talking at that time about farm income, not net farm income. I thought the hon. gentleman had made a mistake, and I pointed this out to him for that very purpose. But the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) intervened as follows:
No, we were talking about net farm income.

What do you
think the farmer is interested in? He is not interested in anything else. The farmer is interested in nothing else but net farm income.

It is quite evident, in spite of the sidetracks that the hon. member for Essex East is trying to go down, that the Leader of the Opposition, as I say, deliberately tried to make me appear to know nothing of what I was talking about. To cover up his own obvious mistake he did it deliberately, apparently, because he had those two hours to check his blues and prepare this new statement which he made. This is the type of thing which I think is completely irresponsible, the sort of thing which causes those of us who pay attention to these matters to lose complete confidence in members who follow that sort of practice.
As a matter of fact, following that he gave what he purported to be the correct figure. He said that $100 million was not enough. He checked it up; he admits he checked it up during the dinner recess, and he said it was $181 million. Well, once more, if he is talking of net income, which he apparently says he is, he is still completely wrong. Actually, I have the figures which I have had prepared by-
Look up your own returns.

-the department as to what the net income was for the period 1946 to 1956, and the average for that period is $1,424.7 million, which is $147.1 million more than the net income in 1958, not $181 million. Well, as I said at the beginning, the hon. member, except when he was quoting directly from me or from the Current Review, has used hardly one correct statistic or made one valid statement.
You have not challenged any of them yet.

I think, Mr. Speaker, the point is elementary; it is just a matter of
The Address-Mr. Harkness simple arithmetic and either the hon. member cannot, or his staff cannot, do simple arithmetic, or they do not want to do it. It is either one or the other.
That sounds more like it to me.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
You should get into this
debate.

The Leader of the Opposition indulged in a considerable tirade on deficiency payments for hogs and eggs, which merely demonstrated that he does not understand the basic concept of price support by means of deficiency payments. I might point out to him that deficiency payments have now been in effect for a year, and two years in some cases, for a considerable number of our commodities. I might give as some examples soybeans, Ontario winter wheat, wool and sugar beets; they are some of the more important. The recipients of those deficiency payments on those products, Mr. Speaker, understand them and have expressed appreciation of them, especially the wool producers and the sugar beet producers. I have a considerable number of expressions of appreciation from those people on having put this system of deficiency payments into effect to support the prices of their products.
The basic concept of deficiency payments as a method of price support is that the producers are guaranteed a support price for the year. To the extent that their average returns fall below this guaranteed price the difference is made up by deficiency payments. The payment is not guaranteed for each individual sale made, as the Leader of the Opposition seemed to be arguing that it should be and complaining that it was not.
And as was promised.

No, it was never promised; it was never in anybody's mind, and the people who have had deficiency payments on these products in the past year or two years know that is the situation and so does anybody else who knows anything about it. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, such a system as the hon. members opposite seem to be talking about, that there should be deficiency payments made on each sale, is one which administratively would be just hopelessly expensive. And more important than that is that there would be no incentive to the farmer to get the best possible price for his crop. For example, if we had a support price of $30 for a hog and the farmer could sell his hog for $5 and know that he was going to collect another $25 to bring it up

The Address-Mr. Harkness to $30, there would be no incentive for him to try to get $20 or $25 for his hog. He would not care.
You have to have a system of this kind if it is to be workable at all; otherwise the taxpayer is going to pay the great bulk of the return to the producer for his hog. It is an absolute essential, and everybody who knows anything about this has always understood it. That is the way and the method by which deficiency payments operate both here and in other countries.
At page 57 of his remarks in Hansard the Leader of the Opposition was dealing with hogs, and I would like to quote what he said. He said the government now has a surplus of 201 million pounds of pork, and he purported to be quoting this from the Department of Agriculture's Current Review. He said, at page 41-I might say, Mr. Speaker, he cannot even get the pages right, for it is not on page 41. It appears on page 42.
That is terrible.

Apart from that most minor of the mistakes he made, the statement is just not correct. He should have noticed that this Current Review was put out in November, 1959; therefore it could not give the quantities the government held at the end of the year. All it could give was an estimate, and it is on page 42 where this matter is dealt with. In the column headed "1959 b" we find:
Estimated except for stocks at January 1, 1959.
That is what I said, an estimate.
No, you said we had a surplus at that time-
On a point of order, the minister has challenged the accuracy of the statement I made. Perhaps I can read the exact statement in Hansard at page 57.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is just trying to take up my time and save himself from this criticism.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will give the Leader of the Opposition an opportunity immediately the minister finishes his speech.
Read from page 57.

Page 57; I will read it again. The Leader of the Opposition stated:
The government now has a surplus of 201 million pounds of pork.

Mr. Speaker, that is not what it says on page 57. Perhaps I may be permitted to read the text now, in view of what the minister has said. It reads:


The Department of Agriculture Current Review, page 41, estimates that 201 million pounds of pork had accumulated at December 31, 1959-
What is wrong with that?
If they were estimates-
Why do you not put it right?

If they were estimates, why did the Leader of the Opposition make this statement which I just quoted, and I quote it again:
The government now has a surplus of 201 million pounds of pork.
As estimated. That is what I said. Why do you not use the right words?

This is absolutely wrong. He just does not understand the situation. That is the total stocks in Canada, not the stocks the government held. As a matter of fact I can give the house the exact amounts the government held on that date. At the end of the year the exact amount was 139,770,834 pounds. The Leader of the Opposition said we were holding 201 million pounds. What he does not understand, as I said, is that these are total stocks; that there has to be a pipe line, as it is called, of pork in the hands of the retailers, the wholesalers, the cold storage people and the abattoir people, and this generally amounts to around 40 to 50 million pounds. Therefore he is completely inaccurate in saying that the government now has a surplus of 201 million pounds of pork, and this has created a completely false impression throughout the country. This is another of his extremely irresponsible and incorrect statements.
Better leave it to Paul.
The Leader of the Opposition went on from there to accuse me of bringing on the surplus situation as far as hogs and eggs are concerned by increasing the support prices for purely political purposes.
I wonder whether the minister would permit a question before he leaves that particular matter of deficiency payments.

I am not leaving it. I am
going to be on it for a long time.

Would he explain the quotation recorded on page 58 of Hansard for January 18, 1960, which is taken from page 2581 of Hansard for April 10, 1959:
We will pay the farmer the difference between what he gets in the market place and the price support announced.
Will the minister explain that?

Yes, I will explain it very
readily. I was speaking there of the farmer

The Address-Mr. Harkness as a whole, which we do very frequently, around the country promising higher support The Leader of the Opposition is merely trying prices to farmers in an effort to buy votes, to raise a dialectical argument.	Mr. Hees: And lower taxes.
You deceived the Canadian farmer.

There has never been any
deception. There has been no confusion in the minds of people who understand the deficiency method of payment with regard to how it was going to be carried on. In fact it has been in effect for two years on a considerable number of commodities. There is no question about that at all.

You should be more careful
of your language.

As a matter of fact, after
the terrific number of misstatements the Leader of the Opposition made I think he is the first one in the house who should take that advice himself and be more careful of his statements and his language. On page 57 of Hansard for January 18 he said:
What brought about this startling increase? Last year the Minister of Agriculture was not saying that this was brought about under a Liberal policy. Instead he was taking every credit for bringing about this 201 million pounds surplus.
Of course this is completely wrong. There was no surplus of that amount a year ago. There was no surplus at all a year ago.
That is right. You brought it about.

Therefore this is another
complete misstatement.
The increase was brought about because of the fact that on April 1, 1958, without consulting farm associations, the support price was increased to $25 for purely political reasons.
That is about as wrong as it could possibly be from every point of view. Practically all the major farm organizations made representations with regard to what the support prices should be not only for hogs but for eggs and all kinds of commodities at the time the stabilization bill was being debated in the house, and after it had been debated, and not one of these organizations ever recommended any decrease in support levels. They all recommended that they should be considerably higher, and so did hon. members opposite. They were complaining bitterly because the support prices on eggs and hogs were not high enough, not that they were too high but that they were too low.
With respect to the charge that the increase in the support price for hogs was made for political reasons, I would point out that it was announced after the election, not before. At the same time, during the election campaign the Leader of the Opposition was going
Mr. Speaker, we could have announced these support prices while the campaign was on but we did not do so. We did not make use of such a tawdry device as the Liberals actually did in 1957.
Shame, shame, shame.

The Liberals did that in 1957, so 1 can understand why the Leader of the Opposition thought in the back of his mind that we might have done it. But this was self-accusation. As a matter of fact, in 1957 the Liberals increased the support price to 17 cents a pound for spray processed dry skim milk powder shortly before dissolution of parliament, and at a time when the election campaign was really already in swing. Shortly afterwards they announced a support price of 23 cents a pound for fowl. They announced both these prices for political purposes only. As a matter of fact, all our troubles with regard to skim milk powder have flowed from that action. The farmers did not ask for 17 cents. As a matter of fact the farmers asked for 14 or 15 cents a pound as a support price for skim milk powder, but for purely political purposes the Liberals established a support price of 17 cents a pound before the 1957 election. This was one of the most irresponsible actions of which any government has ever been guilty-
Did you oppose it? You said it was too low.

-because they did not put on import controls at the same time. The result was that when I took over as Minister of Agriculture I found that supplies of milk powder, not only production in Canada but imports from abroad, were mounting up and up. Milk powder was being shipped into Canada by every producing country in the world because of this high support price. It was a completely irresponsible act, and it has taken us right up to just a few months ago to correct the situation and get out of the difficulties caused by this action, which was entirely and purely political.
Did you not ask for a higher price at that time?

The same thing is true with respect to the support price announced at that time for fowl. So much for the charge that the support prices we established were put on for political purposes. Contrary to

The Address-Mr. Harkness the record of the Liberals when they were in office, they were put on after the election and not immediately before it.
Hear, hear; in a very honest way.
I hope that does not get into Hansard.

Mr. Speaker, if you study the experience in Canada and the United States the inescapable fact is that agricultural price support by the method of purchase has proved a costly failure in the case of many products. It has not only not solved the problem of giving the farmer fair prices over the long run, but it has accentuated that problem and made it more difficult to solve.
That very statement by you is a repudiation of your own policy.
Ours is just the reverse.
You ought to resign.

Mr. Speaker, this is so because support by purchase does two things. It provides a floor price and a guaranteed market. The government is obligated to purchase all the product at the floor price. The result is that farmers produce to the utmost of their capacity without any regard as to how or where the product will be marketed. Inevitably the result is an unmanageable and unsaleable surplus in these circumstances. The method of purchase is the method the Liberals were using, and it was as a result of the programs they had in effect for skim milk powder, eggs, hogs and so on that we got into the difficulty we are in. Our policy has been reversed. We have been getting away from these things. Having recognized these facts, when we brought in the stabilization act we made provision for support by other methods than that of purchase, and during the past two years we have been employing these methods more and more, particularly deficiency payments. The use of this method for the support of egg and hog prices to the producer is not well understood, and to clarify the matter I should like to deal with the present egg situation in some detail.
One o'clock.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is one minute past one. I allowed the minister to continue, without objection from the house, because his time expires then.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Hull.
Has the minister completed his speech? We understood at the recess he had something to say about eggs, and I am sure the house would be glad to give him time to complete his remarks.

I have, as I said, a statement on eggs which is in some considerable detail, and a few other remarks which in total might take about 15 minutes. I do not believe I should take advantage of the kind offer of the Leader of the Opposition and so trespass upon the consideration of the house. I shall find a future opportunity, fairly shortly, to deal with these other matters.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, allow me first of all to congratulate the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) on the neatly turned speech he delivered in faultless French, which commends itself to the attention of the house.
I should like also to congratulate the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Cassel-man), who had prepared a lovely speech that was matched only by her personal loveliness. We listened to her with delight, and found that indeed, according to the English; she was
(Text):
-a chip off the old block.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, we are all glad to see you again performing your duties of conducting the business of the house with the same unfailing tact and kindness.
I take this opportunity also to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) for replacing you as Deputy Speaker of this house and committee chairman. I know that he has now acquired enough experience to carry out those duties most creditably. If he follows your example, he can be sure that every one will be satisfied with the way he conducts the business of the house.
Many developments have taken place since last session, Mr. Speaker, and I do not intend to list them all. One of those happy events was the appointment of last year's deputy speaker (Mr. Sevigny) to the office of Associate Minister of National Defence. I take this opportunity, even if he is not here right now, to congratulate him. He is a friend of mine and I hope that he will discharge his duties with tact and earnestness. I ask him to excuse us if we must

attack him at times, but we shall do it in good faith, in the same way he would if he sat on this side of the house and we were in his place.
Apparently, there has always been in this house a representative of the Quebec premier. When Mr. Duplessis was in office, we had the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), our Solicitor General.
Under Mr. Sauve's premiership, his representative seemed to be our Associate Minister of National Defence, since he went as far as announcing the Quebec election in a speech he made in Toronto.
Now there is a new government in Quebec, with a new premier, and since there is a vacancy in the cabinet, maybe the Prime Minister would consider it only fair to appoint a representative of the Barrette government, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). In fact, has he not been Mr. Barrette's secretary for quite a while? He knows him, he knows his ways and he could very easily be his representative in the cabinet.
Mr. Speaker, there is another event which has focused the attention here and there, and that is the very notable by-election in Russell. Perhaps was it only a by-election, but the Conservatives behaviour led to believe that they wanted to make it something like a small-scale general election, so as to make up for their loss of the election in Trinity.
So much did the Conservatives want to make it a general election that for the campaign they mustered at least a dozen ministers who covered the constituency, making speeches and even personal campaigning.
Some thirty Quebec members of parliament spent about a fortnight in the constituency sharing the work in the various communities.
I had the opportunity of running across the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. He had undertaken to win over the Liberals to the Conservative principles.
Thank God, he did not get anywhere, nor the others for that matter. But not only did those thirty members or so and the ministers mentioned tour the constituency, but they made promises. Never in my life have I heard so many promises and wild statements as I heard in Russell constituency. Furthermore, I saw so much money being spent there that one can hardly imagine how much, which proves that the Conservative party wanted to win the Russell by-election at all costs. I even saw an ex-minister of the crown-the ex-secretary of state-campaigning in East-view where he said: "If you want to get something, you had better vote Conservative; if you vote Liberal you won't get anything."
The Address-Mr. Caron And just to give them an example he would say: "Take Mr. Caron, for instance. He wants a bridge. Well the people in his constituency voted Liberal, and they won't get the bridge."
I am quite prepared to believe that this was not an expression of government policy. I am prepared to believe that the Prime Minister wouldn't go that far. Don't you agree, Mr. Speaker, that it is a very inconsiderate form of politics, to travel all over a constituency, making such promises? And if this kind of thing had the approval of the Prime Minister or the cabinet, it would be a very bad concept of democracy, because democracy requires that even people in the opposition be entitled to all essential and necessary services. I am sure therefore that this is not in accordance with the views of the Prime Minister.
And, to prove that the intent was to make it a small general election, after the election, a prominent party member told me that they were fairly confident of winning the race, adding: "If only we had had a better horse." Therefore, the fault was not with the horse, but with the party backing it.
The people of Russell are close to the government. The constituency includes workers, professionals, executives, businessmen, farmers and civil servants. The constituency is made up of people from practically all walks of life but, being located close to the government, its people know what goes on in Ottawa. That election, which was fought as though it had been a general election, clearly shows to the Prime Minister that he should now go a bit further and consider calling a general election so as to give the people of Canada an opportunity to tell him whether or not they are satisfied with a government of deficits and irresponsibility, a government that is apparently blind to its responsibilities.
