Mr. Speaker, as was reported in the press and as stated by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) when he addressed the house: "The speech from the throne is much more remarkable by its omissions than by its contents".
After the Leader of the Opposition had made his usual remarks on the speech from the throne, the Prime Minister announced certain specific measures. Mr. Speaker, this is an indication of lack of courage. It shows how much the Prime Minister was afraid of the power of the opposition, since it had succeeded in demolishing the speech he had given the Governor General to read. He came up with something new: the revision of the standing regulations. Everybody agrees that this is necessary, in so far as the contemplated revision is not a political one, designed to favour the government only, or again a revision of the standing regulations with a

view, perhaps to curtailing the debates in the house. A revision should give an equal chance to the opposition to voice its opinion. Everybody agrees, everybody approves such a thing.
He referred to the amendments to the constitution, to his intention of asking London to let Canada make a final decision, from now on, on all matters of amendments to the constitution. This amendment, as far as the provinces are concerned, had once remained unchanged because the government of the province of Quebec, at the time, opposed it, fearing that the rest of Canada might infringe upon the rights of the province of Quebec. Lately, I heard that the new premier of Quebec said he was prepared to accept such a change. Well, Mr. Speaker, I also am happy to see that, finally, the province of Quebec, under a disguised Conservative administration, has finally decided to join definitely with the rest of Canada.
Reference has been made also by the Prime Minister to the establishment of a royal commission, a Hoover-type commission, on civil service matters. We are in favor of such an inquiry; in fact, we favour an overall inquiry of the whole administration. We want to find the best possible administrative methods in all fields. However, about this matter of the civil service, I feel that the most urgent need now is to think of the fate of those people who, at this time, are having all kinds of difficulties in supporting themselves. We see today many people who are living in almost impossible conditions. Some civil servants, because of their insignificant salary, are forced to work at night as accountants, others as office clerks, others as typists. Some are even forced to work as barmen and waiters, and I know some of them. Those people are not doing this extra work because they like it, but because they are forced to do it by the rise of the cost of living and by the instability they are in because of their low salary. We urge the government to give immediate consideration to this problem. I am not asking the government to revise all salaries, as I understand that would perhaps be impossible. I know that all federal civil servants wish to obtain a salary revision, even those whose salaries are fairly high, because, having been used to a somewhat different standard of living that they have to maintain, it is necessary that their salaries be increased. I also recognize that specialists should get higher salaries, because if we do not pay them adequately, they will go to the United States. Those two categories of civil servants are perhaps
The Address-Mr. Caron able to provide for themselves more or less adequately, but what about the lower paid civil servants, those with children and who, because of the cramped quarters they have to live in with their large families, are unable to make both ends meet?
A federal civil servant, father of nine, told me recently that out of his monthly salary of $249, there hardly remained $200 to look after the needs of his family, after deduction of pension fund, insurance, etc. If a monthly rent of a $100 is deducted from that amount-because a family of eleven persons requires a fairly large house, which cannot be rented for less than $100 a month- there remains for the head of family hardly $100 a month to feed and clothe his children, to heat his house and to meet other expenses, as medical fees, drugs, etc. Therefore, he is left with a bare average of less that $25 a week to provide for all his needs.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, a situation such as this is a physical impossibility, and I believe that a government that tolerates it behaves immorally.
We find that the cost of living has substantially increased since the last depression we had under another Conservative government, from 1930 to 1935. It is a recognized fact that we went through a depression at that time; it is true that the government had reduced civil servants' salaries by 10 per cent, but in spite of that, the cost of living had been dropping consistently, so that just the same we could look after our needs.
It will be recalled that, back in 1932, a house could be rented at $20 to $25 a month. I myself was living in an apartment costing me $23 a month; it had three bedrooms, a living-room, a dining room and a kitchen. Of course, I had to pay for the heating. But today, one could not rent the same apartment for less that $60 to $75 a month.
With regard to clothing, in 1932 we could get a decent suit of clothes for $21 or $23; nowadays, the same suit sells from $65 to $85, and those of better quality, which used to cost at the time around $35, now sell for at least $125.
With regard to food, at that time beef was selling from 15 to 25 cents a pound; now the price varies from $1 to $1.45 a pound, a price three times higher than the one we used to pay in 1932.
I am not asking that civil servants' salaries be trebled, because I admit that, during the depression, salaries were about sufficient,

The Address-Mr. Caron but I want the government to consider the case of small wage earners, those who barely get along, who earn $3,000 a year and whose take-home pay, after taking care of their pension fund, their insurance premium and a government bond, amounts to no more than $50 a week. I am speaking more particularly of those who get small salaries, because as I said a few moments ago, the others can always manage to get by with some effort and hardship. We have to look after those small wage-earners who are starving, while the government is looking at the situation, unable to find the means of solving the salary issue.
I have here copies of employment offers which have been made to the people for some time now, and if we look at the qualifications required we see that university level is prescribed for jobs carrying a salary of $3,750, $4,350 and $4,020 a year respectively. What were the salaries in 1958? I asked for information, because I wanted to know what federal civil servants were getting less than $3,000, $4,000 or $5,000 a year. These are the statistics I have been supplied with.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset to associate myself with the congratulations already extended to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) on his appointment as Deputy Speaker, and also to the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) and the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) on the splendid addresses delivered in moving and seconding the throne speech this year. I would also like to convey to the Quebec members the deep sorrow of those in Coast-Capilano constituency over the great losses suffered by the people of Quebec during the past year in the death of two great and distinguished Canadians while premiers of that province. But in doing so I would also like to bring to the members from Quebec a message of congratulation on the extremely splendid manner in which they stabilized their situation and performed in the traditions of responsible parliamentary government in a most commendable fashion. We welcome the new premier of Quebec and wish him long years of successful administration.
I should also like, Mr. Speaker, to join with the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) in his remarks of congratulations and thanks to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) in bringing to fruition the talks which are about to begin under the chairmanship of our distinguished and beloved Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), a native of our own province, in connection with the negotiations with the United States concerning the Columbia river.
While I am in a mood for congratulating, Mr. Speaker, I should also like to pass on congratulations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the members of his cabinet, who are also practising what I should like to term a very high and responsible duty in administering the government of this nation. In this I refer to the manner in which he and his colleagues considered the report submitted at the termination of the last
284	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Payne session of this parliament by the committee on mines, forests and waters, in which the recommendation was made that this nation should have a department of forestry.
I noticed that the previous speaker, the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) perused the details of the throne speech, but it is with regret that I find his vision has failed him; for certainly here, if in no other place, there is great substance. I quote from the speech from the throne, as follows:
You will be asked to authorize the establishment of a new department to be concerned with affairs relating to the forests of Canada.
I would point out it is not surprising that the hon. member for Hull and those of his party have difficulty in finding substance in an announcement such as this; for in checking the minutes of the mines, forests and waters committee, as conducted during the days of the Liberal regime, I find that it sat, considered and reported after about one, two or three meetings. Never during the course of the former administration have I found that at any time that committee considered matters concerning the forests of this nation.
That, of course, may not be of too great interest to those hon. gentlemen, but in order to keep the record straight I would like to point out that in the year 1957, in gross value of production, the forests and the by-products that come from the forests of Canada were responsible for over $4 billion of Canada's gross national product. I think this, Mr. Speaker, is a very major part of Canada's economy.
Also, Mr. Speaker, in 1957, of total exports in dollars and cents of $4,839 million, the forests of Canada produced exports in excess of $1,456 million, or were responsible for producing more than one third of every export dollar earned by this nation. In 1958 a similar pattern was seen. Our total exports were over $4,830 million. Exports accountable for and produced by the forests of this nation were $1,413 million, and again accounted for one third plus of all the dollar earnings of this nation.
I have no final figures for the year 1959, but for the 11 months ended last November the total export figures show a sizeable increase over the previous year, being $4,584 million for the 11-month period. The forest industries of Canada accounted for $1,381 million, and again represent over one third in dollar value of all the exports from this nation. It is quite conceivable that the hon. member for Hull finds this of no interest, but if these are his thoughts I am sure they are not shared in my part of Canada.


I should like to point out at this time that Canada is approaching its 100th anniversary. Back in the early days of exploration of this continent explorers reported to their native lands, in all cases that there were two great assets to be found throughout the length and breadth of the known area of the North American continent. These were primarily forests and rivers. Last year the government of Canada recognized the need of vitalizing and appraising the energy sources of Canada, and included in that consideration, will be the vast potential hydro output of our rivers. Now in the year 1960 the government has promised to bring into being a department to serve Canada's major export industry, the forest industry.
I think it would be superfluous to go in great detail into the facts and figures surrounding this great industry, for they are familiar to practically anyone who lives in our land. I do feel that it would be advisable for us to consider at some length at this time what the proposed department of forestry can and should do for our nation. It should be made clear at the outset that no one in this house, I am sure, and certainly no one on last year's mines, forests and waters committee has ever entertained any concept whereby the proposed new department would in any way infringe upon the traditional and constitutional rights of any province.
As all members are aware, an industry that provides one third of Canada's exports in dollars and cents is a sensitive industry, an industry which reflects market conditions not only on this continent but throughout the world. Forcibly brought before our committee last year were the conditions of the United Kingdom lumber market. In a very brief way, in the past three years, the export of finished and raw lumber to the United Kingdom market has fallen from the point where once it was Canada's role to supply 20 per cent and, in some years 28 per cent, of the timber and lumber used by that nation is reduced to a point where last year it only constituted 10 per cent of the total imported by the United Kingdom.
In an effort to find out the reasons we discovered that a great many market factors come into play. Russia had entered the United Kingdom market and was selling on contracts embodying what is known as a fall clause. A fall clause, and I am perhaps overgeneralizing again for the sake of brevity, means that the Soviet union will deliver timber to the United Kingdom market at a price guaranteed to be below that of any other supplier at any given period. It is rather difficult for Canadian exporters to

compete when an undercutting of their bottom price is guaranteed by contractual commitment on the part of the U.S.S.R.
Norway enters the picture in a rather major way as far as United Kingdom imports are concerned. That country has an advantage over the Canadian exporter because of the shorter water haul. The greatest importer of Canadian lumber and far and away the greatest importer of Canadian pulp, raw, finished and in newsprint form, is the United States. From our studies last year we found that while, for instance, in the pulp field consumption by the United States market had increased 141 per cent over the past five years, Canada's exports had increased in this market, only 45 per cent over previous exports to the United States.
The state of Texas is an illustration of what is affecting that market. Up to only four years ago the vast consumption of pulp and newsprint in the state of Texas had been entirely supplied by Canadian sources, but in the last three years that market has been lost not only in part but wholly. Why? The answer is that scientific methods and the study of seeds and species of trees have brought into being forests in the southeastern section of the United States that produce a soft pine which today sustains a pulp industry that has replaced this traditional market of Canada.
To return briefly to lumber, I think it is surely right to say that the welfare and health of the pulp and paper industry, certainly in the province of British Columbia, is almost entirely contingent upon the health and productivity of our lumber industry; for in British Columbia, unlike most other areas of Canada, our pulp mills are supplied largely by waste from lumber production in the form of wood chips and sawdust. The falling off, of lumber, as I indicated earlier, in the United Kingdom market has had a very direct effect on the cost and the supply of raw materials to our west coast pulp mills.
Hon. members have asked me in discussions I have had with them-I am sure if the hon. member for Hull bothered to concern himself with the welfare of Canada's major export industry he might well ask the same thing- what a federal department of forestry should undertake to do and what role it can play. Certainly the first phase this would have to do with the administrative field, but a major and paramount need in the nation today is forestry research. We have a very minor undertaking in the forestry branch now administered by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Likewise we have a scientific study of forestry being conducted by the federal Department of
The Address-Mr. Payne Agriculture. But I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that this industry, involved in woods operations and forest production, have great difficulty in finding one central source to which to come for information. This certainly holds true of the forestry branch, operated on a very limited scale, under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. One of its interests are the forests in our national parks. The industry runs into a great deal of trouble in having long term, scientific studies undertaken in a successful manner through the Department of Agriculture.
I say this without criticism, because it is merely human for ministers of agriculture, past, present or future, to consider that their role is concerned with agriculture. Should that be done, then a canal through Chignecto could become a vital artery for the transportation of northern ore to its destination in eastern smelters.
More recently, Mr. K. C. Irving, one of Canada's and certainly the maritimes' leading industrialist, made a speech on Chignecto when he addressed the maritime provinces board of trade on June 18, 1959. It is a rare occasion when Mr. Irving makes a public speech; I understand that this was one of the first that he made to a large maritime group. He stated, according to press reports:
Failure to build the canal following confederation promises dating back to 1864 and 1866, he charged, had "destroyed our coastal shipping and industry."
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, this is entirely a federal problem. However, I suggest to the government that before any more money is spent on the St. Lawrence seaway the Chignecto canal should be given priority. During construction millions of dollars will be spent to the benefit of the people in the area. It is now understood that this canal has been accepted as a logical extension easterly of the St. Lawrence seaway.
The second of the three C's is equally important and has also been discussed in this house by many maritime members. I refer to the New Brunswick-Prince Edward Island causeway. This will probably cost in excess of $200 million and take several years to complete. During construction it will prime the economy of the two provinces and when completed give the public proper transportation facilities. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) spoke on this subject in this house on April 20, 1959. At that time the hon. member for Queens was discussing

The Address-Mr. Creaghan transportation generally and what he considered to be his interpretation of the confederation promises. He is reported at page 2842 of Hansard of that year as follows:
To mitigate against our separation and insularity great emphasis was placed upon the matter of communication. A situation was to be created whereby we would get all the benefits of a direct link with the Intercolonial and other railways which were being projected at the time. The disadvantages of our isolation were to be overcome, and on that basis the colony of Prince Edward Island entered confederation in 1873. The terms of our agreement are precise on this question-
The hon. member for Queens then quoted from the agreement of 1873. That agreement can be summarized as follows: the dominion government was to assume full responsibility, winter and summer, for an efficient steam service for the conveyance of mail and passengers. If we go back to 1873 it is only fair to state that it was then impossible even to speculate that a causeway could be constructed across this body of water. However, it is equally fair to assume today that what was to be an efficient steam service is not now sufficient.
The third "C", at the present time considered by some to be of lesser importance, is a roadway from the province of New Brunswick across the state of Maine to Sherbrooke in the province of Quebec. This has been referred to as a corridor road. In order to construct such a roadway there must be the fullest of co-operation between the governments of Canada and the United States, and between the provincial governments of Quebec and New Brunswick and the state government of Maine. It certainly is justified as a project that would greatly improve the transportation situation between the maritime provinces and upper Canada. It also should be considered by both governments as a route in case of disaster or for civil defence evacuation. In any case an immediate start on one or more of these major federal works programs would go a long way toward bringing about economic equality to these provinces by the sea.
Much has been accomplished in Westmorland during the past two years by this government. My constituents and myself are very grateful for everything that has been done. It is unfortunate that time does not permit me an opportunity of making a complete review. The departments of government concerned are familiar with these projects, and I want to take this opportunity to thank publicly all those who in any way assisted me during the past two years. However, there is still a long list of projects urgently needed. For example, the people in the town of Sackville need and have requested a new public building for this town. The present

post office facilities are most inadequate and there is a long list of patrons awaiting post office boxes.
The board of trade and town council have been corresponding with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hark-ness) about the public offices now located in this town. It is hoped that the Department of Public Works will proceed immediately with the purchase of a parcel of land on which to erect a new public building large enough to house the present offices and services in Sackville and to look after future needs of the various departments.
On January 7, 1960 I attended a joint meeting sponsored by the Sackville board of trade and town council. I have here a copy of the resolution which was forwarded to the Minister of Public Works by letter from the board of trade dated January 11 and I think it is important that some reference be made to this resolution. I quote from this letter as follows:
The meeting, which included Mayor J. W. Rose and members of the town council finance committee, unanimously endorsed a resolution instructing the executive council of the board of trade to write you stressing that there is no major difference of opinion as to the desirable location of the new federal building to be built in Sackville. It is the earnest wish of the residents of the town that this building be constructed in a central location, chosen by the federal authorities concerned, with particular emphasis placed on the need for sufficient space to house other government agencies besides the post office, and taking into consideration possible future expansion in so far as this is practical.
The residents of Sackville were greatly concerned because of rumours that certain government offices might be moved out of this town. I can assure this honourable house that the ministers responsible have co-operated 100 per cent with the town council and the board of trade and have indicated individually that moves are not now contemplated.
Since prior to the war another town in my riding, namely the town of Shediac, has been without a public wharf. This town is located entirely on the coast, containing approximately 3,000 inhabitants. Recently a plan was proposed and submitted to this government whereby the town of Shediac and the provincial government had offered financial assistance to the harbours and rivers branch of the federal Department of Public Works. By this plan the town council would contribute $16,000, the province of New Brunswick $24,000 and the remaining expenditure for this wharf, estimated to cost

$160,000, would be paid by the federal government. Two months ago further consideration was given to this suggestion which was first made in June, 1959. As a result of further discussions it has been ascertained that a cheaper wharf can be erected. This alternate plan, like the former one, has been agreed to by the town and, I understand, has been agreed to by the provincial government. If the federal Department of Public Works can now agree to this most recent plan- which, by the way, will cost the federal government less than $50,000 as opposed to the one of June last providing for an amount of $120,000 the residents of this town on the coast of Northumberland strait will be satisfied that once again, after a period of 20 years, a wharf to satisfy their fishing and personal needs will be erected.
The largest employer in Westmorland is the Canadian National Railways. Since becoming a member of the House of Commons I have experienced the fullest co-operation from the officials of this railway. Although I stated that I have received the fullest cooperation, I cannot say that I am in complete agreement with its policies. Recent lay-offs at the C.N.R. shops at Moncton is an example. It was reported in the Moncton press that the Atlantic region is the only C.N.R. region that is making a profit. This statement was made in Moncton on Thursday, January 21, by an alderman, who also emphasized the fact that business does not usually lay-off its employees when it is making a profit, but only where it is showdng a loss. I feel it is my duty to take advantage of this opportunity once again to urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the senior officials of the Canadian National Railways to reconsider this recent lay-off, and in the future to make definite plans to stockpile work in order that such large lay-offs will not again occur.
At the present time the province of New Brunswick is the only province in Canada that has not a C.N.R. hotel or a hotel in which the C.N.R. has an interest. On behalf of the citizens of New Brunswick I urge the board of directors of the C.N.R. to make plans for the erection of a new hotel in my native province. I feel quite confident that once a favourable decision has been made it would only be natural that this hotel would be built in the city of Moncton, the transportation and railway centre of the maritime provinces. Only when that day arrives will it then be correct for this hotel chain to state and advertize that it is the Canadian National Hotels Limited.
Mr. Speaker, in bringing my remarks to a close I want to take this opportunity to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) for his wonderful assistance and
The Address-Mr. Winch co-operation in 1958 and 1959 when he was Minister of Public Works. During this period of time the Department of Public Works decided to erect a large extension to the existing federal building at Moncton. The original building was constructed in 1936, and to date there have been two additions. The proposed extension for 1960 will add nearly 73,000 net square feet and make available much needed space for various departments of government now in the present building and rented accommodation throughout the city. This will be one of the largest constructions undertaken in this city for some period of time, and reflects the progressive growth and importance of the fastest growing city in the Atlantic area.
The final edition of the Gordon report of November, 1957, in the chapter entitled "The prospects before us", has this to say, and I quote from page 15:
We suggest that some of our increasing national wealth should be used to facilitate adjustments that would make the economy stronger and more resilient; to knit the various parts of the country more closely together; to finance developments that would indirectly promote economic growth and permanently add to the country's assets; to assist regions that may not be keeping pace with the economic progress of the country as a whole; and, finally, to encourage Canadians to participate more fully in the economic growth of their own country.
I suggest that this quotation can be referred to as my own personal interpretation of what I consider to be the national development policy of this government. As a result of this quotation it seems obvious that we in the maritimes received the benefit of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant, which has already been of such great assistance.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I am quite certain that the outlook for New Brunswick, and Westmorland in particular, is very bright for 1960 and the years immediately ahead.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to make my contribution to the address in reply to the speech from the throne I will first of all honestly admit, that perhaps even more than heretofore I am finding it a little bit difficult for my tongue to express the words and thoughts which are in my mind. However, basically, I think I can put it this way, that in my estimation at this session this year we are facing, or should be facing, one of the most difficult times in history. As far as the present session has gone, starting with the speech from the throne, it is my belief that the government as a government, and ourselves as members of the House of Commons, have not faced up to the economic facts of life or the realities of the world situation.
296	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Winch
I believe it is correct to say that the present era could be characterized as one of anxiety: anxiety in the minds of aH people; anxiety in the minds of all countries. The conditions in the world today-and that includes Canada of course-are too dangerous for anything but the truth. Much as I regret it, I do not believe that we in Canada, in this House of Commons, and in the government, are facing up to the truth, the real truths, the fundamental truths.
That, perhaps, is understandable, and is human nature. The government wants to remain in office and maintain its majority. The members of parliament, irrespective of party, want to hold their seats; that is understandable. Industry wants to maintain, and if possible increase its profits. Labour wants a greater share of the wealth which the workers produce. All these things, Mr. Speaker, are human nature and are understandable. But being understandable is not good enough if we, in this session, irrespective of the party we represent; if we in Canada irrespective of the economic phase we represent, think from a personalized individual or personalized organizational basis. I am afraid, whether we agree or disagree, whether we are popular or unpopular, that that is what we are doing, and it is the biggest mistake that we could be making at the present time.
May I begin, after that introduction, by referring to the speech from the throne which in my estimation is one of the most innocuous documents I have ever heard or read. It failed to face up to the realities or to the facts, and gave very little information concerning the important matters which will come before us in the next six or seven months. As a matter of fact, we got a lot more information regarding the business of this house when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke than we did in the speech from the throne. But even when the Prime Minister did speak I say, with all respect, that the government still failed to face up to the world situation today and the problem of Canada's own position in present world circumstances.
We know, and the Prime Minister informed us, that defence estimates are to be referred to a special committee. That was welcome news and it was interesting, but it was not what the people of Canada were expecting. They had anticipated an explanation with regard to Canada's defence policy. The crossfire which went on for hours between the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) during which these two hon. gentlemen read quotations from the past and condemned each other was not what Canada needs today in order to understand


defence policy and planning. It is welcome news that the Prime Minister intends to have a special committee appointed to inquire into defence expenditures, but he made it clear- and I draw this particularly to the attention of the house-that there could be no discussion of policy.
In that case we are not going to get very far, because instead of an honest discussion this can only lead to a bit of window dressing. I think I know whereof I speak because, I believe, it is only a year ago that defence expenditures were before the committee on estimates of which I was a member. That committee sat for weeks, and what happened? Any time a member wanted to call witnesses to give evidence, unless it met with the approval of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes)-which it never did-no witnesses could be called. Any time it came to a question of policy as regards expenditure, what did the committee get from the Minister of National Defence? We were told that this was a matter of policy and we were ruled out of order. We had that experience just over a year ago.
What is needed today is not window dressing but a full understanding of defence policy and the need for expenditures which have been advocated. I am very glad that the Prime Minister is here. In the two speeches he made in answer to the Leader of the Opposition the right hon. gentleman made confusion worse confounded as far as his policy and attitude are concerned. Praise was given to the Minister of National Defence on account of actions which have been taken in the last 18 months because, it was said, we are now in the missile age. But what did the Prime Minister reply when we asked him to comment on the speech made by the president of the United States to the effect that the major threat is still the manned bomber? There was no answer. But it is important to try to put these two things together-the statement made by the president in his budget to congress and the statement made by the Prime Minister in this House of Commons.
If it was right and honourable to refrain from comment-and I am not questioning that at all-we still have not the answer from the Prime Minister of Canada as to defence policy. If we are in the manned bomber age, why the cancellation of the CF-105; and if we are in the missile age, as the Prime Minister has stated, why spend $300 million on the Bomarc, which, if United States reports are correct, is as yet untested. If they are not correct, how is the Bomarc going to be used in the missile age when it is a defence against manned bombers?

These are definite questions to which we think the people of Canada are entitled to answers, and the Prime Minister's speech with regard to them is a mass of contradictions. We think that $300 million could perhaps be better used by the senior citizens of this country and by the veterans rather than being spent on a weapon which is obsolete and useless.
We are living in an age of anxiety. It might be interesting, it might be intriguing, and it might provide news for the press to see members of the opposition and the government battling back and forth about how many unemployed there are in Canada. It would be interesting to know how many, but the most important thing is not whether there are 400,000 unemployed or 800,000 unemployed, the important thing is that there are unemployed. That is the problem; that, and what is being done about it.
A great deal of patting on the back has been done with regard to the winter works program. According to a report in the papers this program is going to mean the employment of 14,000 persons in Canada. But what about the others? What about unemployment insurance? The present payment is not enough to keep a person at anywhere near a decent or adequate standard. Moreover, there are thousands of people who are not entitled to these benefits under the present regulations. Day after day, before I left my own constituency, I came across cases where men were short a couple of stamps and therefore not entitled to insurance. Here in Ottawa, in my office men have approached me with a similar problem.
Irresponsible nonsense. Of course, when they are short of stamps-
You try to get along with your patronage. I cannot, in the opposition.
Be responsible.
You had your chance. Now I am making my speech. I have often been amazed, Mr. Speaker, how those with the narrowest minds have the widest mouths.
Would the hon. member please inform this house-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Unless the hon. member who has the floor resumes his seat, it is not customary to interrupt.

I only take my seat, Mr. Speaker, when you are standing.
As I was saying, grave problems confront both those who are receiving unemployment insurance and those who are unable to get it, a number of whom have visited me in my office since I came to Ottawa. They are relying on the Salvation Army to take care 79951-0-20
The Address-Mr. Winch of them. They cannot do it forever. Thank God they do have some period of time when they can assist.
We are facing serious problems with regard to those who are on fixed incomes, the senior citizens, the veterans and those on superannuation. There is no mention in the throne speech and no mention by the Prime Minister or any cabinet member of their problems, their anxieties, and whether or not any action is to be taken to give them some relief; none at all. There are anxieties on the home front; there are anxieties on the defence front, there are anxieties on the international front.
I said that we had to face up to truths. One of them I am going to be honest to admit. I think I realize and recognize I did not know all of its complexities until I had the privilege-and I do mean privilege-to be elected as one of the five members of parliament to attend the biennial conference of the commonwealth parliamentary association in Australia this last fall. There, Mr. Speaker, as you so well know, being the leader of that delegation, we had the opportunity of meeting with 130 delegates from 48 parliaments of the British commonwealth. There can be no question, or at least there is not in my mind, that in the minds of some, if not all, that personal prejudices and preconceived ideas and dogmatic thinking abounded at our first meeting together. But as a result of getting together and talking, living and travelling together there came about an understanding of each other, of each other's country and of each other's problems and aspirations. The result was that when the conference was finally held in Canberra there was talking straight from the shoulder on problems, and out of that talk there was, I think, the unanimous opinion that one of the great problems facing us today is aid and assistance to the underdeveloped countries. There was not only this consensus as a result of the biennial conference, but there was that opinion in the other countries outside the commonwealth as well that we were privileged to travel through. It is here that I want to add that we are not facing up to it.
I want to be the first one to say that on a per capita basis I think Canada is making a greater contribution to the Colombo plan and outside the Colombo plan than any other country in the world. I want to make that as the first statement; but I do want to say I regret that in the speech from the throne, and the speech so far from the Prime Minister, we have had no announcement from Canada that we are going to give a greater leadership and make a far greater contribution to the undeveloped countries of the world.

The Address-Mr. Winch
The reason I feel there is so much importance in this is that there is an unofficial revolution taking place in the world, namely the emergence from the cocoon of colonialism of the Afro-Asian countries. Any person today who still retains any idea of white superiority had better get rid of it fast because the Afro-Asian countries are not going to be quiescent. Without doubt, in my estimation, in the next ten years they are going to be a major factor in the world, and the position of Canada is going to depend to a great extent on the basis of understanding and friendship which we lay down today. I am certain that the majority-let me put it that way-of the Afro-Asian countries in their emergence, in their fight for freedom and self-government, desire to follow the precepts of the free world, but they face what almost seems to be insurmountable problems. They need not only help but a great deal of help, and there are only two ways they can follow, namely the precept of the free world or the concepts of the totalitarian world. Although I know, sir,- I wish I were wrong-it would not be a popular position to take in Canada, it has got to be taken.
This parliament and the people of Canada have to be told of the meaning of this Afro-Asian development as it is now and as it certainly will be in the next ten years. Canada has of necessity now, if we are going to maintain our position of security and standards, if not to improve it as the country with the second highest standard of living in the world, to sacrifice and be prepared to sacrifice in order to assist not only the underdeveloped countries in the commonwealth but the underdeveloped countries in the rest of the world. This involves major support to those countries seeking to follow the precepts of free countries and democracies which are facing a great deal of difficulty.
I was never so proud as I was when we arrived in Indonesia to find the reception we got because, if I remember correctly, Canada was the first country that ever made any offer of assistance, which was done last year. Capital assistance, education, teaching in trades is an absolute essential. Incomplete as it may be, I want to say that there is an international truth that we have not properly faced up to yet, and the speech from the throne does not give any evidence that we intend to this year.
Perhaps one of the big failures of the government and of the House of Commons is that the people of Canada have never been taken into the confidence of the government and of parliamentary democracy and given an explanation as to what is taking place, the problems and difficulties that lie ahead


and our responsibility, not only for meeting them ourselves but in helping others to meet their situations. I think this should be a year of truth.
As I said, I think we are too complacent and I definitely think the government is too complacent, especially in regard to our economic situation in Canada as an exporting nation. There is too much political expediency from the government side of the house instead of honesty. Let me give you an illustration. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made a speech to the Canadian club in the Royal York hotel in Toronto on Monday, January 11. The last paragraph of his speech contains this sentence. I have a transcript of his speech here:
The message which I should like to convey to Canadians at the threshold of this new year and decade, therefore, is a challenge in simple terms: "Work and Save".
Then, we received through the mail the speech of Mr. McKinnon, the president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, in addressing the 93rd annual meeting of that bank. He says on page 2:
The rapid recovery from last year's recessive phase has been generated largely by consumer expenditures which through the year continued to be a source of strength to economic activity.
Now, sir, we have the Minister of Finance and we have the president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. I think the government deals with the Canadian Bank of Commerce. I know I do and I appreciate their assistance and co-operation. The president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce and the Minister of Finance have absolutely different views of the situation. The people should be told, which is correct. Let us have no diatribes, no cross-fire across the floor of the house, no references to what the Liberals did or did not do and what the Conservatives said or did not say when they were in opposition. What is the recommendation as to credit and financial policy?
What goes for finance goes for trade. There was a brief sentence in the speech from the throne on trade and a very brief reference was made by the Prime Minister. But, sir, may I, through you, tell the Prime Minister and the government that the issues are not going to be resolved by patting themselves on the back, by admiring each other as they sit on the front benches or by quoting statistics on exports, imports and national production. There are many other factors involved and not only can figures lie but liars can figure, to use an old saying.
What are the factors that we are facing overseas as an export nation and what are we

doing to meet the situation? I maintain that we are not doing enough, are not saying enough and are not planning enough. We were glad to hear the report of the Minister of Finance on behalf of himself and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) on their return from Paris but we got very little information as to what it may mean as far as the inner six and the outer seven are concerned. It was with a great deal of interest that I read a report from Sweden a couple of days ago that there is going to be a major effort to shut out the Atlantic countries inside of a year. But we have not been told what the effect could be to Canada and how we are going to meet the situation.
Most important of all we certainly have not been told on the basis of the knowledge of the government-they must have a lot more knowledge than private members- what their analysis is of the economic cold war of the U.S.S.R. and its satellites. I have no hesitation whatsoever, in saying that there is not going to be a fighting war. That may sound like a very dogmatic statement but in my humble estimation there is not going to be a fighting war between the free world and the U.S.S.R. because they know what it would mean to them if they ever tried it and the United States knows what it would mean to them if they ever did so. It is not necessary because the U.S.S.R. can achieve what it wants on the basis of its present policy by means of the economic cold war.
The U.S.S.R. has absolute control of its industry and what goes into the home market and what goes into the export market. It can use one phase to counterbalance the other and it is able to adapt its production for home consumption or export according to the policy of the government. They are demonstrating the effect they can have on the markets of the world under a totalitarian, planned economy. I do not have to use my own figures as to how the province of British Columbia is affected. In the Vancouver Province of December 17 last I find the following:
In 1951 Russia exported 168,000 standards of lumber to the U.K., while the share of 34 B.C. mills in that market was 346,000 standards. In 1959, it's estimated, B.C. shipments to the U.K. will be only 165,000 standards, while Russian exports will be a sizeable 400,000.
In other words, in 1951 British Columbia shipped 200 per cent more standards of lumber to the United Kingdom, one of our good markets, than the U.S.S.R. while in 1959 the U.S.S.R. shipped 250 per cent more to the United Kingdom market than did the province of British Columbia. I do not 79951-0-204
The Address-Mr. Winch profess to know the answer but I do say that the government, with its sources of information, its economists and analysts, should take the house and the people of the country into its confidence and tell us how we are going to meet this competition under a capitalist system and maintain employment in Canada and our exports abroad.
We also have to face a situation that I admit some people have not liked me talking about but any time a member of parliament is not prepared to accept the responsibility of speaking on things as he sees them it is time that man was no longer a member of parliament. I have found that some of the big importers from Canada are disturbed by economic instability as they put it. In other words, they are worried whether or not there is going to be a continuity of supply to meet their needs and because they feel they are not assured of that guarantee, consideration is being given, I am told, to a reduction of some imports and importing from the Scandinavian countries and the U.S.S.R.
I am a socialist, and believe in the objective of democratic socialism but because I have that objective for the future, which I am going to strive with all my might to achieve, I am not idiot enough to forget that as long as the majority of the people vote to support capitalism we have got to live under it. That is why I think it is the responsibility of the government to take the House of Commons and the people more into its confidence with respect to our problems and difficulties and their plans to meet them.
I want to emphasize to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and everyone on the government side that they will not get co-operation and consultation required to meet our world trading problems as long as governments are battling labour, as long as governments are bringing in anti-labour legislation, as long as industrialists are making the biggest profits they have ever made in their lives and damning labour and creating suspicion. Government, industry and labour have responsibilities in 1960 and mighty big ones. The situation is not going to be solved by attacks and creating suspicion. It is useless for an industry to ask labour to hold the line, as was done in British Columbia a year ago, damn labour, and say that they cannot give an increase in wages, and then the next year declare profits 60 per cent higher than the previous year. Do not take my word; that is a quotation from one of the leading business executives of British Columbia.

The Address-Mr. Winch
I do not believe, sir, the government can find the final answer. I know it has not got it because you have to have a planned economy to be able to find the final answer. However, in this interim period we have to keep our people at work, and this means there has to be responsibility by government, responsibility by industry and responsibility by labour. I regret that the Prime Minister has not seen fit to take any action on the request made by Mr. Jodoin of the C.L.C. in Toronto to get together the representatives of industry, labour and government, to try to thresh out their difficulties and their differences, to try to achieve a basis of understanding. If industry is not prepared to place an effective limit on profits, then the government will have to do it through the medium of price control and through the medium of excess profits tax.
Labour is now practically under wage control because you have to have negotiation; you have to have a government conciliator and you have to have a government arbitrator. Wages are pretty well under control. If workers' labour power is to be controlled, then why should there not be some control of prices and of profits? I say if industry will not do it then it is the responsibility of government.
I have stated, and I know I am correct, that we can maintain our standards in Canada but we can only do so on the basis of honesty, understanding and the acceptance of responsibilities. I believe very definitely that this is so, and I say it should be the responsibility of government at this session to recognize that whilst management claims their profits are not too great and blames labour for the high cost of goods, whilst labour in turn states wages are too low and management gouges the customer thereby reaping excess profits, the way to resolve this is for the government to establish a competent, unbiased commission to study the relationship between prices, wages and profits, with particular emphasis on the relation between wage increases and price maintenance.
I notice that my time is now practically up, so may I conclude in this way, perhaps ineffectually, by trying to indicate my interest and concern in the Canadian economy and its relationship to the rest of the world. I would say that I agree with the statement that the western world, with all its riches, all its know-how, cannot continue to exist with three quarters of the world illiterate, impoverished and diseased. Therefore, although it may mean sacrifices by the Canadian people and the Canadian treasury, in the long run it will prove to our benefit in

friendship and added democracies if we make those sacrifices today. Although I am an avowed socialist I believe in practicalities and may I say through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Prime Minister as the head of the government that our main business is not to concentrate too much on what lies very dimly in the distance but to do what lies closely at hand and there is much that requires to be done.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPORTING OP INTERJECTIONS-RIGHTS AND PRIVILEGES OF MEMBERS
speechtext:
Before another hon. member takes the floor, I wish to raise a matter which affects the privileges of the members of the house. A reference in Hansard, as it comes from the reporters, has been drawn to my attention. This covers an interruption which is unparliamentary. While the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) was speaking, an interruption was made while I was not in the chair and which, perhaps, was not heard by other members in the house, but was heard by the reporter. One hon. member interrupted with the words, "Vous mentez", which, in English, means "You lie", and is recognized as an unparliamentary interruption. I am sure that if such an interruption were made, perhaps with the concurrence of the hon. member this interruption might be stricken from the record before it appears in the printed text. This could be done with the concurrence of the hon. member to whom it is ascribed and by the unanimous concurrence of the house.
It seems to me this would be the wise course to take because otherwise this remark, which perhaps was made by inadvertence, will appear in the printed text and I am sure the hon. member would wish to correct it. Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to congratulate the Deputy Speaker. His well-known ability, his poise and tact particularly qualified him for the duties of Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons and chairman of the committees of the whole.
I also want to commend the mover (Mr. Morissette) and seconder (Mrs. Casselman) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The hon. member for Rimouski, who is a noted economist, stated the economic problems of the hour with precision and clarity. He pointed out the efficiency of the remedies applied by the government, and the proof may be found as the hon.
The Address-Mr. Martineau representative so aptly said, in the fact that today, we are not facing a recession any more, but a new period of stability and prosperity.
The house has certainly lived through one of the most pleasant moments of its history when the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas stated in her clear voice and with all her known eloquence, some of the truths of which it is proper to remind not only hon. members, but certainly also all elements of the people. I am therefore happy to offer my most sincere congratulations to the hon. member.
Mr. Speaker, before making a few remarks on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I would like to take up some of the words the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) said this afternoon. When he was speaking the hon. member reminded me a little of the mountain which gave birth to a mouse. I am not saying this with malice with regard to the hon. member for Hull who is one of my best friends, but I think he is sometimes mistaken, and that it would be right to say that he is sometimes trying to make us believe that the moon is made of green cheese. When saying this, I am thinking more particularly of his remarks with regard to the civil service in this country and especially in respect of salary levels of federal employees.
Just as he did last year, the hon. member told the house that there are -civil servants who are starving in his constituency. Those are his very words.
Before going into the matter of salaries paid to government employees, I wish to pay tribute to that group of Canadian citizens. They work for the welfare of the nation, and I would even say that the country could not be run without their help. I feel that without them, the leaders of the country would be powerless.
While paying tribute to this group of devoted -citizens, I should like to show, with all the fairness that such a problem calls for, just what is the situation of those people.
The hon. member for Hull painted an almost tragic picture of their situation. He told us how much the cost of living had gone up since 1932, and how, as a result of the steady increase in the cost of living, these people are in an extremely difficult position. First of all, let us bear in mind that during the whole period to which the hon. member for Hull has referred, his own party held power for 22 years.
304	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Martineau
And it was while that government was in power that the cost of living increased the most. On the other hand, he said that during the Liberal administration the civil service had been granted six or seven successive increases. In spite of that, he claims that civil servants are now facing a situation which is not very different from that of those who are starving. That amounts to saying, therefore, that the increases granted to civil servants under the previous Liberal administration were not adequate for, since our party has been in power, the cost of living has gone up only 3 per cent.
Furthermore, he said that we had not granted any increase to civil servants. Now, we granted them a general increase in 1957, and since then, we have, several times, granted other increases to certain categories of employees. Therefore, those are two flagrant inaccuracies which must be pointed out.
I am sure the civil servants understand the present situation; they are convinced that the government is doing everything in its power to settle that problem in a satisfactory way, considering the means at our disposal and considering also the other classes of our society. And the government will continue, until the inquiry announced last week has taken place and made its recommendations to revise those special categories which deserve increases which seem more indicated than in the case of others.
Therefore, that is the way the hon. member for Hull, no doubt in good faith, is creating a false impression. I know myself, from the discussions I had with several civil servants, that they are generally satisfied with the government's efforts to settle their case, and that they are awaiting the results of that inquiry before any settlement or final decision is arrived at.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great satisfaction that I found out in the speech from the throne that the government is considering the establishment of a department of forests.
The hon. member (Mr. Payne) for Coast-Capilano has outlined the advantages of such a department. May I only recall that the history of the whole Ottawa valley since the beginning is related to the forest. I shall go as far as to say that we would not be here perhaps if the forest had not brought about the first development in this area.


The first settlers in the Ottawa valley were woodsmen. In fact, the forest inspired the folklore of this valley, the history of its pioneers, of its heroes who opened up a new empire in the Ottawa valley and along its tributaries such as the Black river, the Coulonge river and the Gatineau river. Then, I am sure that this new department will play an important part in insuring that our forest products continue to rank first among our exports.
In the speech from the throne, the emphasis was mostly on the development of the natural resources of our country. I am glad of it. On the question of development of our resources, I wish to draw the attention of this house on a project which was often put forward here. I am thinking of the dredging of the Ottawa river.
The industrial superintendent of the city of Ottawa recently drew up a report on the importance of this project. He showed how these last years the rate of growth of the city and district population was increasing continuously. Thus, last year the population of the city of Ottawa was over a quarter of a million, and it is expected that by 1964 the population will have increased by 90,000. In the near future, the population of the area will be close to 500,000 people and if we are to provide for the needs of that increase in population, so that the possible developments of the city and district of Ottawa are not jeopardized, I think that we should seriously consider the deepening of the Ottawa river, and the first step would be to make Ottawa a seaport readily accessible to ocean ships. That could be achieved rather easily and at a relatively low cost estimated by the Ottawa industrial commission in the vicinity of $41 million. Such a project-

for the Carillon dam, sufficient space was allowed for dredging. Certain members of the house know also that the building of a new access bridge is planned on the west side of Montreal island. There also, steps are being taken so as to enable ocean-going vessels to pass under that bridge.
This is a very worthwhile project from which the area will benefit greatly.
When the hon. member asked me his question, I was saying that not only the city of Ottawa would benefit from it, but also the entire area to the northwest and to the east of Ottawa, and by this area I mean all the territory to the northwest of the Ottawa river, as far as North Bay, through North Bay and up to the Timiskaming riding on the Ontario side, and to the Temiscamingue riding on the Quebec side, and the mining centres of Rouyn, Noranda, Val d'Or, as well as the Chapleau, Abitibi, Pontiac and Gatineau ridings.
You are aware that the production of this area is considerable; it is mainly forest products and by-products. The companies already operating will no doubt be able to reduce their costs through the use of such a seaway; furthermore, we must take into consideration the increasing importance of the mining industry in northwestern Quebec.
We already have mines producing iron, zinc, lead, gold and silver. Besides, the prospects are excellent for the production of other iron mines, when we think of the value of the Vincon deposits, in Pontiac constituency, and at Ironside, in the constituency of the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron).

All these industries could benefit from such a project. The city of Ottawa could foresee an industrial future equal in that field, to that experienced by cities like Toronto and Montreal.
Besides, it would be the first phase of a great dream of the pioneers of the Ottawa valley, that is the dream of seeing the whole Ottawa river system become a seaway from the island of Montreal to Georgian bay.
But, for the present, I will be content to urge the authorities to consider the first step, that of the dredging of the Ottawa river from Montreal island up to Ottawa, as well as the construction of harbour facilities necessary to Hull.
Another point which was mentioned last week by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) himself, has stirred up great interest.
The Address-Mr. Martineau
It has to do with the proposed amendment to the constitution. I should like to express entirely personal views on this subject.
First of all, everybody agrees, and it is the natural prerogative of a sovereign nation, that one should have the right to amend one's constitution.
On the other hand, it is not normal and it would certainly not be fair that parliament itself be entitled to carry out constitutional amendments, because, after all, it would mean the violation of a certain principle, that of the specific value of the constitutive act, which is beyond ordinary legislation.
Now, if the parliament of the country is able to amend its constitution by itself, it follows that the constitutive act itself is reduced to the status of mere legislation.
This is true in a general way under any system, but more so under a federal system which has somehow emerged following agreements or pacts between different provinces and various ethnical groups.
It would be entirely abnormal if this parliament, though sovereign, had the right to amend its constitution at will and on its own.
On the other hand, the British authorities have certainly neither any interest in maintaining the power which is now conferred to them, with regard to amending the constitution from a federal point of view, nor any wish to do so. As a matter of fact as stated by a certain columnist the Imperial government has acted through the years as a mere notary, that is to say that it recorded the will that was expressed, that is the will of the Canadian nation to amend its constitution and endorsed it.
Now, I would suggest as a means and simply as a proposal designed to stimulate discussion, that a constituent assembly be set up and instructed to bring to the present constitutive act substantial amendments, or else revise or recast it completely, in order that our constitution may become a twentieth century legal instrument.
I would suggest also that the members of such a constituent assembly be not elected but simply appointed, in part by the central government and in part by the provinces, and that such an assembly be empowered to bring the amendments I have indicated to the constitution, that it be empowered also, should it deem it proper, to recast it completely, but only under certain conditions. In other words, such a constituent assembly could not bring any amendment to the rights affecting provinces and

The Address-Mr. Martineau minorities, as they are described under sections 91, 92, 93, 133 and others of the British North America Act.
Only with the unanimous consent of the federal government and of all the provinces could amendments be made to such rights or provisions.
Following the submission of a report by this constituent assembly, its draft constitution would have to be ratified by the Canadian voters in order to become the law of the land.
Moreover, the point here concerns not only the revision of the constitution, but also its interpretation. And at the present time, the Supreme Court of Canada is the body which interprets constitutional points.
With all due respect for the supreme court, which is certainly an illustrious court and has been doing a great job, it is certainly unhealthy that this court should be called upon to settle differences between the federal government and the provinces. Conflicts of interest may arise between the federal government and the provinces. However, as the members of the supreme court are appointed by the federal government, it seems to me that there is something wrong there, in the sense that certain principles which are regarded as sacred under British law are apparently not being followed. I mean that justice need not only be rendered, but it must be rendered in a manner which is obvious to all.
So I again suggest, with regard to litigations between the federal government and the provinces, and also in matters involving the constitutional validity of a federal or provincial act, that a new court be set up to deal with such cases. Such a court, which might perhaps be called a constitutional court, might be composed of one judge appointed jointly by the federal government and by the provinces.
I think this might be an improvement, and perhaps more important, it might bring about better understanding on federal-provincial matters.
And finally, as a last remark on the subject of constitution, I should like that the bill of rights, when it is adopted, be incorporated into our constitution or be made an integral part of our present constitution or of the reviewed constitution.

With your kind permission, Mr. Speaker, I will now continue in the English language. Certain congratulations were offered at the start of my speech and I forgot to congratulate one member of the opposition. It is unfortunate that he is not here. I refer to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. 

Pickersgill) who last fall, in the course of a very successful and well-attended Conservative convention, obtained a very distinguished award. That award, was given to him as being the person who had contributed most to the success of members sitting on this side of the house who come from the maritime provinces. It was stated that had it not been for the frequent incursions of that hon. member into their respective constituencies during the course of the last two election campaigns several of them would not be here.
It was unfortunate, however, that the honoured recipient of such an award was not able to be present personally to receive it. He was otherwise engaged. I believe he was engaged in the compilation of the memoirs of a former prime minister of this country, but although he was too busy to attend that week he was nevertheless able to come to the city of Ottawa the following week to attend a meeting of the advisory council of the national Liberal federation. I hope that as a result the long awaited publication of the memoirs, which members of the house are anxiously awaiting and which I am sure posterity will long cherish, will not be too long delayed.
I should like to dwell a little on that famous Liberal meeting that was held in Ottawa in December because there are certain amazing things that were said. First of all I should like to talk about some words uttered by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who stated, almost with emotion choking his voice, that every measure of social legislation on the statute books had been placed there by a Liberal administration. Then he went on to say that our administration had stolen Liberal ideas in the field of social legislation. That is quite a novel idea indeed because I do not believe that ideas can be stolen. They belong to everybody. Ideas are part of the great universal heritage. This places us in a dilemma. On the one hand, these ideas are either worthless or else they are worth quite a bit. If they are worthless then of course they cannot be stolen because according to the Criminal Code a thing which has no value cannot be stolen. There is a certain minimum value placed on an object before it can be stolen, so I do not know if these ideas can be stolen. *
On the other hand, if these ideas have a certain value, then how can hon. gentlemen sitting opposite object if we appropriate them because they would then be contributing to the general welfare. I think that hon. gentlemen sitting opposite wish, in their own way of course, to contribute to the welfare of all. But there is more to it than that. I do not believe that people who live in glass houses

should throw stones. I seem to remember that often the C.C.F. party used to accuse the Liberals of stealing their ideas in the field of social legislation. How often were Liberals dubbed C.C.F'ers taking their time or was it the C.C.F'ers who were called Liberals in a hurry? I do not know whether it was one way or the other, but I certainly know that today such thinking on the part of the Liberal party must give rise to a lot of deep thought.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) once said that the Liberals certainly were not the party of the right, that they were to the left, although he said "We are right of course; you know what I mean." But at the same time, he did say that they were to the left. We have another great party of the left that is in the advance stages of gestation and will certainly soon be brought to life. If it does come to life, then I just wonder what will become of that great Liberal party; I wonder if they will simply, like the Arabs, silently fold their tents in the middle of the night and steal away.

speechtext:
Then, there was that famous Liberal convention. If ever a modern Gulliver should appear, he certainly would like to visit that, especially when the Leader of the Opposition told his party stalwarts that Liberals must never be satisfied with the contemplation of past achievements. These were, I opine, words of wisdom because in such an attitude there lurks two dangers. On the one hand, there is the great danger that they may consider anything which may have been accomplished in the past as springing from their own virtues. This is a type of narcissism which is sinister and dangerous and with which hon. members sitting opposite appear to be particularly afflicted.
There is also the danger that one's vision even of things at hand might become blurred and one cannot then fully comprehend the achievements of the present and the promise of still better things for the future. It seems obvious, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members sitting opposite have fallen into both of these pitfalls, and I heartily commend the Leader of the Opposition for his timely words of warning to his lieutenants and party supporters.
However, the Leader of the Opposition went even farther, and I must commend him
The Address-Mr. Martineau for his words of paternal admonition when he said that Liberalism has to gird not only against the Tories-this I might say is a Herculean task-but also against the inertia of human nature and its acquiescence to what is customary and usual. These are surely words of highest wisdom. The inertia of human nature-let us think about this. What a striking example of this inertia we have in the gentlemen who sit opposite who have refused to move with or accept progress, who delude themselves into thinking they are still in the times of the docile Liberal majority and who would push back the clock to recreate, were it possible, their days of glory forever vanished. Then the Leader of the Opposition went even farther than that and in a moment of unguarded oratory he stated, and I quote:
This new technique of selling a person and a platitude by all the resources of modern media of communication is recognized as a danger.
When it comes to platitudes, of course, we are no authority to discuss such a subject with the Leader of the Opposition who once defined the art of politics as being the ability to make a platitude sound like a pronouncement. If we accept the maxim that practice makes perfect, some of the hon. gentlemen sitting opposite may soon become experts in the art of politics as defined by no less an expert than the Leader of the Opposition himself.
At the same convention the Leader of the Opposition also revealed his amazing insight into the anatomy of fish, such as would certainly earn for him merited recognition from our learned societies. For example, during the course of his talk he analysed the type of stimulation, not an ordinary stimulation but a five-way sense-stimulating underwater message activating all five senses in a fish brain which hypnotizes the fish into darting straight before the line. I am not quite sure what the Leader of the Opposition had in mind when he gave such a technical, or should we say biological description of the ways and wiles of the fish. Did he mean to say that the Canadian voter was like a fish, to be lured, or that his audience reminded him in some vague way of fish, or did he simply want to imply that he was giving them a lesson in angling as they were wasting their time at that convention and certainly would have passed it much more profitably elsewhere fishing on one of our beautiful lakes.
Perhaps, after all, the Leader of the Opposition and his stalwarts could not speak of anything else but the ways of fish. What
308	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Michaud could they say if they spoke about the state of Canada's economy? Would not the Leader of the Opposition then have had to remind his party followers that he had made certain predictions about a year ago and these predictions, in fact, had not turned out to be as he saw them? He predicted such things as rising prices, a declining economy and rising unemployment. None of these predictions has come true and therefore it is very difficult for the Leader of the Opposition to talk about these things.
Then he started into the field of international affairs. He tried to imply that since his government took power our reputation abroad had diminished, and that it was only in the great days of the past that Canada enjoyed an enviable reputation. Certainly it is admitted amongst the diplomats at the United Nations and elsewhere that never was Canada's reputation higher.
