Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I join with the previous speaker as well as with all those who took part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, to congratulate most sincerely the deputy speaker of the house and chairman of the committee of the whole (Mr. Flynn).
(Text):
I wish also to congratulate the mover (Mr. Morissette) and the seconder (Mrs. Cassel-man) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the able manner in which they fulfilled their respective tasks. It did honour both to themselves and the constituencies which they represent in this house.
I wish at this time to talk about a matter of great significance to all those concerned with the economic advancement of the maritime provinces, namely the need of having the Chignecto canal built. Before any new industry can be expected to establish in any location it must be reasonably certain of a profitable operation. In order to have a profitable operation, it is necessary to be competitive. Unless that is possible you can neither expect new industry to locate here nor established plants to remain, provided they are operated strictly on a business basis and no other ties. For an industry to be of value to a community it must be prosperous. It should have earnings in proper keeping


with capital invested, risks taken and effort required. Otherwise it would have no guarantee of a future and may not be an asset to the community.
A profitable industry requires raw materials, power, transportation and many other things at prices it can afford to pay; and, above all, it requires a market either at home or abroad in which it can sell competitively. We have some raw materials in the Atlantic provinces and, owing to our seaboard location, others are available to us from all parts of the world. We have power at prices not competitive with that in Quebec, Ontario and some other parts of Canada but for some industries it is available at reasonable cost. Transportation, generally speaking, in these provinces is expensive. Yet the bay of Fundy and Northumberland strait areas could have a most economical system of water transportation, particularly now that the St. Lawrence seaway is in operation. The seaway has created greater opportunities than ever before available to these Atlantic provinces.
The construction of the Chignecto canal to improve transportation as a joint venture by the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island was one of the reasons that brought delegates from the three provinces to the meeting at Charlottetown on September 8, 1864. It was at this meeting that representations were made by Canada, now the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, that instead of a three-province union, it should be a confederation of five provinces. Following this meeting, as an inducement for the acceptance of their proposal, the delegation from Canada offered the promise of the Chignecto canal. This promise was made also at Quebec in October, 1864 when all delegates were present and again at the conference held in London in December, 1866. The promises were never kept. There can be no question that the failure of the federal government to keep those promises has had a great deal to do with the destruction of our coastal shipping and with our high freight rates.
Canada had great difficulty in persuading New Brunswick to enter confederation. There were many of our forefathers who could not see any benefit. They were fearful of what the future under the proposed confederation, would be. The report of the Nova Scotia Jones commission of 1934 explains that Canada's tariff policy has cost the maritimes roughly 50 per cent more than the benefits they have received. To put this in dollars and cents, the net tariff cost to us in the year 1931, one of the depression years, was $10,817,000. No doubt in the years immediately before and after 1931 the net cost

was much greater. I have seen some calculations using a round figure of $10 million per annum with compound interest at 5 per cent. Over a 50-year period the net cost to us would be $2,093 million; for a 60-year period, $3,535 million; and for a 70-year period, $5,885 million. I would ask you to think of what a financial contribution we have made to Canada. This is a credit on which we should be able to draw. The interest alone would build a canal every six months. When you drive through central Canada you can see prosperity everywhere. The people in the maritimes feel very strongly that we have paid for some part of that prosperity.
A meeting of the Progressive Conservative candidates held in Moncton in May, 1957 adopted what were called the Atlantic resolutions. The co-chairmen of the meeting were the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks), and the present Minister without Portfolio from Newfoundland (Mr. Browne). The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Now-lan) was chairman of the committee which drafted the platform. I will read some extracts from the resolutions adopted at that meeting, as follows:
Federal assistance for the Atlantic provinces under a national resources development program, under the framework of a Canada wide policy-
Adoption of an Atlantic capital projects program, to provide federal capital assistance for provincial projects designed to enlarge the basic economy of the area. Such a program would provide for development of the Prince Edward Island causeway, the Chignecto canal and similar capital works designed to aid the economy of the region.
The Atlantic platform also said the Progressive Conservative candidates were committed to the original pledge given to our people at the time of confederation that freight rates would be adjusted and transportation facilities would be provided so that our geographic position would not prejudice our producers in having reasonable access to the markets of Canada. Many voters obviously had a great belief in that platform. But what have those who attended that meeting in May, 1957 done to implement that platform which was then presented to the verdict of maritime voters? As already mentioned, the co-chairmen of that meeting and the chairman of the resolution committee are now ministers of the present government. Many others who are now sitting in this house have also been elected as supporters of the present government.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) stated recently that the cost of the Chignecto canal is now estimated at from $90 million to $140 million, that both engineering and economic studies are continuing and reports should be received in the near future, and
The Address-Mr. Michaud that anyone who has any information about the possible use of the canal should come forward.
Any economic study made today, after our coastal shipping and industry have been destroyed, would show that there is not sufficient available traffic to justify the estimated expenditure. The federal government should take our promise that if they build the canal we will use it to the best advantage, restore industrial activity to the maritime provinces and again place ourselves in a position where we will not be number one on the charity list.
In 1873 Messrs. Gzowski and Keefer, two outstanding engineers, estimated the canal could be built at a cost of $5,317,000. The canal was not built. No doubt the money was used for building other canals and has produced a handsome return for other parts of Canada. That places a dollar sign on the unfulfilled promise to the maritimes. The then estimated cost of the canal, with compound interest at 5 per cent per annum for the intervening 86 years, would now amount to over $353 million. Is it not reasonable to say that Ottawa should make available whatever part of that amount is required for building the canal? Why talk about its cost? Almost 95 years ago the canal was promised as part of the consideration for entering confederation. After all these years we still need and want the canal; Ottawa should carry out Canada's promise.
It is my belief, as it was of the maritimers back in 1864 and 1866, that for the industrial success of the maritimes the Chignecto canal is a must. By many in the maritimes the canal has been about forgotten. Many of our people have become so accustomed to conditions as they exist that they do not realize what the unfulfillment of this promise, twice made by Canada and accepted by us, has cost us. They have lost all conception of what this canal could do for Atlantic industry. Can you imagine the steel plants at Hamilton, Port Colborne, the Sault, Gary, Chicago, Detroit and Buffalo being built and operated successfully without the assistance of the canals on the St. Lawrence and the great lakes or the transportation of iron ore, limestone, coal, and their finished products? I believe that if the Chignecto canal is built the country can depend on us to make good use of it, and later fully justify its building.
Mr. Speaker, the tragic events which brought disaster and sorrow to so many families in the fishing communities of Baie-Ste. Anne, Escuminac and Bay du Vin last spring aroused the sympathy of the whole Canadian nation for this hardy class of Canadian citizens engaged in the fishing industry. The hazards faced in the daily life of a fisherman are now known to all. All

The Address-Mr. Michaud should now be agreed that no effort should be spared to assure the maximum amount of protection to those who toil the seas as their way of life. While we have nothing but sorrow for those affected by that tragedy last spring, we should also be thankful to God that many others were spared during that fatal night. I have been speaking to fishermen in my own constituency who, caught on their fishing grounds by that sudden gale, spent the whole night sailing at random waiting for daybreak to reach shore.
These fishermen all had the same observations to make concerning safety measures within harbours and along landing wharves. First of all, they feel that every harbour should have lighted buoys to indicate the channel course when not otherwise indicated by lighthouses. Second, the position of every landing wharf should be clearly indicated by appropriate sets of lights so as to avoid unnecessary hazards to fishermen having to anchor after nightfall. While some of these landing wharves in my constituency are properly lighted, others are not. Similarly for harbours and channels. The desperate situation of those fishermen already referred to a moment ago was the result of being unable to land in the dark due to the absence of lights, both in the channel approaching their wharf or mooring, and on the wharf itself.
These observations raise another essential point with regard to public safety for fishermen, namely the necessity of adequate landings in every fishing community. In my own constituency many facilities by way of landing wharves were provided during the last decade. However, improvements to these facilities should be kept in line with the increasing volume of our fisheries. While only a limited number of new projects may be required, many others already begun should be pursued to completion. I shall make it my responsibility to bring these matters to the attention of the proper authorities in due course of time.
Then there is also the matter of dredging. The Department of Public Works usually maintains a dredging program which provides satisfactory approach to all these wharves. This is a service, however, necessitated every year by the rapid movement of sand, and I am confident that a thorough survey and soundings will again be executed in every port at the opening of the next navigation season to ascertain where dredging is again required. Mr. Speaker, our fishermen are deserving of every consideration in their toiling and hazardous task of reaping the harvest of the seas.
We witnessed a debate in this house a few days ago which had to do with granting

financial assistance to western farmers who had suffered severe crop losses through the effects of unseasonable weather conditions. Members from all sides of the house unanimously endorsed the measures then proposed by the government. The nature of these measures, however, did not permit a full-scale debate on agricultural conditions in the country. This opportunity should be provided for on later occasions. I would like to state now that this government will be pressed at that time to adopt measures which will be of assistance, not only to farmers of certain sections of the country but to all Canadian farmers from all parts of the country who through acts of God suffer severe crop losses.
Having in mind at this present time the farmers of my own area particularly, I wish to indicate to the government that they, too, have suffered severe crop losses due to unseasonable climate conditions during the course of the past crop year. Following an unusual degree of so-called winter kill, an unusually cold spring and unseasonable harvesting conditions, farmers of my area have harvested what is estimated to be only a half crop of hay and hardly better than a half crop of grain in the year 1959.
I wish to emphasize at this time that as a result of these adverse conditions these farmers feel every bit as hard pressed for cash as those wheat growers whose crops were left under snow. In both instances it is a matter of having made the necessary disbursements for crops which did not reach the farmers' hands. In the case of those farmers in my own area extra hay, when at all available, has to be bought at this time to prevent serious stock reduction; mixed feeds have to be brought in in extra amounts in order to complete field rations. The government may rest assured that government guaranteed loans for these farmers who, for the most part, are also operating at a loss at this time would be just as welcome to them as they can be to any other class of farmers from other parts of the country.
I do not wish to elaborate further on this point except to say to the government that unless it is satisfied to see agriculture declining from a primary to a secondary industry in my part of the country, broader measures of farm assistance applicable to all sections of the country must be considered in the immediate future.

Mr. Speaker, December 21, 1959, has been a memorable day for the Acadians of the maritimes. It is the day French television station CBAFT, in Moncton, New Brunswick, came on the air for the first time, realizing

a dream that has long been cherished by the Acadian population of this region. It has been said of the event, at the time, that it was a Christmas gift. For that gift, I think I may speak on behalf of all the televiewers of station CBAFT to express to the C.B.C. our sincere thanks. But it is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that, according to the saying, there should be a fly in the ointment. It must be said that this Christmas gift has not been of benefit to all. Because of the low broadcasting power of the new station, too many homes cannot receive its signal. It has been, believe me, a cause for deep disappointment in many homes of the area. The situation could be best summed up, Mr. Speaker, by quoting an editorial from 1 'Evangeline, that was published the very day of the opening of station CBAFT, on December 21, 1959. I quote:
The governors of the C.B.C. deserve congratulations for the Moncton station, which will rapidly and efficiently improve its services. With the inauguration, we should be able to say that most of the Acadian population can now see French television. Station CHAU, in Carleton, serves the Acadians in Restigouche and Gloucester. It is true that the station is now bilingual. But everything seems to point out that it will become a French station the day an English station will be built on the north shore. Since three companies are competing for that privilege, the day may not be too far off.
In Madawaska, reference is made to a satellite station that will reach the major part of the area.
Unfortunately, while we are rejoicing today, we are thinking of our brothers who are not so privileged as we. There are all those of Nova Scotia, for instance, including important groups in Digby-Yarmouth and Cape Breton. And also there are those of the northern part of the county of Kent.
When the setting up of CBAFT station was announced, there was much concern about its low power; for the people of Moncton it will be a marvellous thing. But, what about the others? At the time, we were told by way of explanation that the station would reach the 60,000 Acadians of Westmorland, Kent and Prince on Prince Edward Island.
Faced with such arguments, laymen had to hold their peace and wait. As from tonight, we shall know how many of those 60,000 Acadians can tune in Moncton station properly. And we trust that if, for any reason, the station would not cover all the territory ascribed to it, the necessary adjustments would be made.
After all, the C.B.C. has incurred considerable expense to establish the Moncton station. It has obtained the best equipment and engaged 18 people to make it work. It is therefore consistent to expect of the C.B.C. that it be the first to want to give adequate service to that whole area.
Mr. Speaker, all the Acadians in the maritimes are confident that soon now French television will be available to their area. Might I, moreover, suggest that the C.B.C. include in its expansion project for the CBAFT
The Address-Mr. Thomas station, a special room for local programs. It seems that such a station could not be complete unless it contains the required accommodations for local programs, to enable local talent, and we have some, to perform in front of all the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West):
speechtext:
welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate on behalf of the people of Middlesex West. I should like, first of all, to associate myself with the other hon. members of this house who have spoken in this debate and who have extended congratulations to yourself, Mr. Deputy Speaker, on your appointment to your present high office. We have every confidence that you will carry out your duties with dignity and efficiency and so honour this chamber.
I should like, also, to extend our congratulations to those who have been promoted to positions of higher responsibility during the recess: the hon. member for Lon-gueuil (Mr. Sevigny), the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker) and the various members who have been appointed parliamentary secretaries. I should like to add our welcome to the new Sergeant-at-Arms and his deputy. I should like, also, to add our congratulations to those already extended to the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Moris-sette) and the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) on the excellent contribution they have made to this debate in moving and seconding the address in reply.
I welcome the opportunity to reaffirm our continued faith in Canada and in our fellow Canadians. In the 93 years of our existence as a nation we have made notable progress. We are a nation scattered across the northern half of this continent, with our several areas of population separated by natural barriers of water and of sparsely settled rocky terrain. The cost of tying those areas together to create this nation has been high and will continue to be high. We built expensive railways, highways, canals, airlines, pipe lines, and communication lines. In spite of all obstacles and political differences we Canadians and our forefathers have created one of the strongest, healthiest and wealthiest nations in the world today. There is every reason to believe that the present generation of Canadians, together with our new Canadians, will continue this development in a manner worthy of our forefathers.
The opposition parties have moved amendments to the address in reply implying lack of confidence in our government. The amendments charge that the government has failed

The Address-Mr. Thomas to develop and enunciate clear and consistent policies, to provide full and accurate information, to initiate fundamental, economic and social plans and have thereby contributed to the confusion and uncertainty that prevails about certain important areas of governmental responsibility including defence, public finance, agriculture, markets and so on.
As a member of the government party I join with my colleagues in strongly opposing any such amendments. We believe that our government is doing a good, honest, efficient and well-planned job of administration, and we wish to commend them for it.
We in Canada, as in any free enterprise country, face the challenge of proving to the world that our democracy is just as efficient as totalitarianism and more pleasant to live with. We are not without serious problems, but the speech from the throne gives indication that the government is diligent in seeking solutions to our problems.
All government is a compromise. Under our free enterprise system individuals and groups are forever pressing for legislative advantage. What helps one may hurt another. Some producers want freer trade; some producers want more protection. We cannot have it both ways. Those on lower incomes want more generous welfare provisions; those on higher incomes want lower taxes. We cannot have our cake and eat it, too. We cannot all benefit equally through government policies all the time. There has to be give and take. Equity is an ideal that we should aim at but which is very difficult to attain.
We believe that our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and our government have done a good job in preserving equity in our economy, in promoting national unity and in furthering the cause of world peace. As a result of their efforts our prestige in the world has increased, national unity has reached an all-time high. Canada from coast to coast, from east to west and from north to south is united as never before.
We welcome the announcement in the speech from the throne that full voting privileges in federal elections are to be extended to Indians without any loss of former rights and privileges. This is a development which many people feel is long overdue. It demonstrates that this government believes that all Canadians should be equal under the law and that we should have no second class citizens.
I wish to congratulate the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fair-clough) and her officials in the Indian affairs branch on encouraging the formation

of an agricultural committee of Indians on the Muncey reserve in our constituency to promote more extensive cultivation and better use of the land on that reserve. Our best wishes are extended to all concerned for success in this undertaking.
We welcome the completion of a fine new central school on this reserve, a school fully equipped with modern facilities for education. I believe that the officials of the Indian affairs branch are convinced, and I believe that some of our Indians themselves are convinced, that more education is the best means of solving the economic and social problems of these original Canadians.
I wish to commend the government for taking a firm stand in favour of sound money. Inflation, creeping or otherwise, is one of the most difficult problems facing our free enterprise economy. We have been warned by the governor of the Bank of Canada and by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that we are over-spending and over-borrowing. Restraints are required to protect the stability of our money. The Prime Minister and his government have been diligent in urging restraints on all segments of our economy and in seeking to cut down government spending. There has been no lack of clarity and consistency in their attitude to this problem.
The Prime Minister has already placed on the record statements from several bank presidents endorsing the stand of the government on fiscal policy. I wish to quote further from the address of Mr. James Muir, president of the Royal Bank, in his address to their annual shareholders meeting on January 14, 1960. He is reported by the Canadian Press to have said:
Monetary authorities did precisely the right thing in October 1958, when they held the money supply constant in the face of increasing demand for loans. Had they not set about neutralizing the terrific head of monetary steam generated by the previous increase in the money supply, we should have seen an uncontrolled blast of inflation which might well have been disastrous.
The previous increase in the money supply to which Mr. Muir refers is the money which was injected into the economy to bring us out of the recession into which we were drifting when this government took office in 1957. The people of Canada elected this government in 1957, among other reasons, for the purpose of correcting that recession and, in 1958, a further mandate, unprecedented in emphasis, was given this government to proceed with that correction. The correction was carried out. The trend to recession was halted and reversed, and our government is now following financial policies designed to guide our economy on the road to progress with stability.

The government's attitude in this respect is summed up by the Minister of Finance in his speech to the Canadian Club in Toronto on January 11, 1960. This speech has been referred to several times in this debate. The minister said:
In I960 we have neither recession nor incipient recovery. We are in the midst of a period of marked expansion in the Canadian economy. We welcome it, but we do not wish to see it mushroom into a boom which would set loose the forces of inflation. What we must all desire is orderly growth without inflation. That must be the goal of policy in this year of expansion 1960.
Many of our people in Middlesex West regret that there seems no acceptable method of decreasing the present rate of exchange on our Canadian dollars. We are proud of the soundness of our money but the prevailing exchange rates are creating difficulties in our external trade. Our people in Middlesex West export substantial numbers of cattle to the United States and would prefer to see this premium on our money wiped out. The Minister of Finance, in his speech mentioned above, listed several alternative methods that could be used to reduce the exchange rates but stated his belief that the disadvantages of any of these alternatives outweighed the disadvantage of the premium on our money. In other words, to try to cure the situation would be worse than the situation itself.
Some of our people are interested in extending the services of the industrial development bank. I have been requested, as I expect other members have, to press for the inclusion of telephone companies in the list of industries that may qualify for loans from this institution. Several independent telephone companies in our area require capital but find that telephone companies cannot qualify for loans. It is requested that the government give consideration to bringing telephone companies within the scope of the industrial development bank.
I have been notified by several municipalities in our area that they desire the assistance of the national government in preserving the purity of the water in the great lakes. Our government is requested to take all possible precautions that lie within federal jurisdiction to see that pollution of the great lakes is prevented. This action is urged especially in connection with the offshore drilling for oil along the southeastern shore of lake Huron.
We have a number of elder citizens in our area who will welcome the announcement in the speech from the throne that legislation is planned to ease the restrictions on the payment of old age security and veterans allowances outside of Canada. The present regulations have created difficulties for some of these people. The privilege of receiving these
The Address-Mr. Thomas allowances outside Canada would be a source of much satisfaction and convenience to many.
There continues to be difficulty among some of our people in understanding the operations of the Unemployment Insurance Act. This difficulty may be unavoidable but it is suggested that the information available to the contributors under the plan be reviewed for the purpose of providing the contributors with a clearer understanding of what they can expect by way of benefits. Most of the complaints reaching me come from married women who cannot understand why they fail to qualify for benefits under some conditions of unemployment.
There is a feeling also on the part of some of the permanently employed contributors that the public should carry more of the burden of seasonal unemployment. With this atitude I am inclined to agree. Seasonal unemployment might properly be the responsibility of the general public and not the responsibility of a selected group of wage earners. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) during the last session expressed his intention of having this matter investigated. We wish to congratulate him on having this investigation begun and we will await the results with interest.
A number of our industries, among which are textiles and rubber footwear, are pressing for more protection in our home market. This matter was ably dealt with by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) in his speech and I am not going to enlarge upon it further than to say that some of these industries were expanded to meet war requirements and feel that they are now being abandoned. It is suggested that their problems should be given serious consideration with a view to preventing undue hardship or the possible disappearance of these industries.
There has been much discussion about increases in pay for the civil service. Our people in Middlesex West feel that our civil servants should be paid on a par with industry and the professions. We welcome the announcement of the Prime Minister that a royal commission will be appointed to inquire into all phases of our public administration with a view to encouraging operations that are efficient and suggesting ways of reorganizing operations that are not. There are in our civil service many dedicated people who are doing a good job. These people are entitled to all the support elected representatives and the government can give them.
Our people wish me to extend our congratulations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) upon the good will he has created since taking office. He has inspired confidence within our own land

The Address-Mr. Thomas as well as abroad. He carries a heavy load of responsibility for the future welfare of Canada. We are inspired by his success and that of his assistants in persuading the United Nations to undertake research into atomic fallout. We wish him success with his formula for securing agreement on the law of the sea. We are confident that under his leadership Canada will continue to exert a powerful influence for disarmament and world peace.
The financial difficulties of our railways are continuing. These problems, arising out of our changing patterns of transportation, are difficult to solve. We cannot do without the railways and yet it seems impossible for them to compete without some measure of subsidization. The report of the royal commission is awaited with interest and we wish to commend the government for appointing this royal commission.
We greatly appreciate the assistance of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and his officials and the officials of the C.N.R. and the board of transport commissioners in expediting the construction of the Hutton side road underpass in London township. This construction is progressing steadily and should be completed within a few months.
We welcome the intimation in the speech from the throne that additional funds will be made available for building homes under the National Housing Act. These funds should be available well in advance of the opening of the construction season.
Commendation is due the Postmaster-General (Mr. Hamilton) and his departmental officials for conducting continuous surveys in areas of new development in our cities with a view to extending house-to-house delivery as soon as any area reaches the necessary density of population, the standard required being an average of 40 yards between delivery calls. Several areas in Middlesex West close to the city of London are approaching this standard of development and should be able to qualify soon for house-to-house delivery.
The planning of a new post office building for Strathroy is much appreciated by the people there. We hope that the negotiations for a site satisfactory to the town and to the Department of Public Works will soon be completed.
Our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) has vigorously promoted the policy of the government to obtain for the farmer a greater share of our national income, and I would point out that the government's policy in this regard has always been most clear and consistent. Changes in the methods of supporting the prices of some commodities have had to be made to prevent the accumulation of

excessive surpluses while giving the maximum support to the family size farm.
Some of our large producers of eggs are hard hit by the recent drop in price, but it is hoped that this condition will soon be remedied as it was in the case of the turkey market. Turkey producers suffered a similar experience with low prices for several months in 1959, but during recent weeks turkey prices have returned to a more satisfactory level and the turkey industry is looking forward with confidence to a good year in 1960. It is suggested that agricultural commodity groups and governments should give consideration to the advisability of extending production management regulations or controls to be devised and administered by the farm commodity groups themselves, with a view to bringing production into line with market requirements. The Ontario flue-cured tobacco growers marketing -board has been successfully applying production controls. It is suggested that other commodity groups could profit from this example.
Many of our farmers are hoping to obtain financial help in reorganizing operations through the new farm credit corporation. This legislation can be of great benefit to agriculture in Canada. The policies followed in administering this legislation will have an important bearing on its success. It is suggested that the regulations should be flexible enough to allow scope for a variety of enterprises and for small as well as large operations. It is suggested in this connection that small holders who depend partly on wages and partly on farming for their living should not be overlooked. It is suggested also that a means test or other safeguards should be incorporated into the legislation or regulations to prevent exploitation of this legislation while the interest rate remains low in relation to commercial rates.
Many people in Middlesex West are interested in federal assistance for conservation developments planned by the Ausable river valley conservation authority. Flood control in the Ausable watershed is of great importance in the counties of Middlesex, Lamb-ton, Huron and Perth. The urgent item at present is construction of the Parkhill dam. This dam is required to control flooding on thousands of acres of rich vegetable growing marshlands below Thedford. A new bridge on provincial highway No. 81 in the vicinity of the proposed dam site is required, and the structure could serve as a dam as well as a bridge. The provincial department of highways has deferred the building of this bridge for some months on the chance that a saving could be made by combining the bridge and the dam. The town of Parkhill,

adjacent to the proposed dam site, is badly in need of a new water supply which could be attained by the construction of this dam. This project which could All three important needs, is being deferred pending a reply by our national government to the application from the Ontario government for federal assistance. This project is not in the class of the Saskatchewan river development or the Columbia project, but it is a genuine effort in the field of conservation. Our people are hoping that their plans to control the ravages of nature on the Ausable watershed, which will cost several millions of dollars to complete, will merit national support.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to take part in this debate on the address may I be granted the right to express, on behalf of my constituents and myself, the great feeling of joy which we have in seeing you back in your office in such good health and, possibly, with determination. I should like, as many others have done, to extend congratulations to the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) upon the contribution which she had occasion to make earlier in this debate, although we all realize, especially on this side of the house, the feminine affection which she bestowed upon the party to which she belongs.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, allow me also to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) on being appointed Deputy Speaker of the house, as well as the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) who was given the opportunity of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne in French.
(Text):
In speaking tonight on behalf of the constituents of Nickel Belt I do feel that I represent the people who constitute a typical Canadian riding. I mean by that that we are, and have been for many years, favoured by one great industry which has brought to this country much wealth and prosperity. The majority of my people are workers in mines or on construction. I have also many farmers and a few small business people. I do not, as some other members do, represent a great metropolitan centre where major manufacturing progress may be expected. However, progress has been noticed in northern Ontario since it was opened up over 70 years ago and there is room for much more expansion. Possibly some day we may see some major centres there, too, as we do in other parts of Canada.
My speech tonight in the debate on the address in reply will be made having in mind
The Address-Mr. Godin the class of people I have mentioned. These people in my area have seen a reduction in construction which has been very detrimental to them. Our farmers are caught in the cost-price squeeze problem of this country, and of course the small business people in Nickel Belt are hit by the tight money situation and high interest rates.
As I begin these remarks, I must confess the surprise I have felt during the course of this debate in hearing members of the government refer to the last election, which took place nearly two years ago, as an argument. When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was speaking in this debate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made such a reference, that the people had given the answer. Again tonight when the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) was addressing remarks to this house we heard the cry that the answer was to be found in the victory of two years ago.
May I stress, with all the power I have, that there should be an end to this administration trying to find a cliche answer to all the mistakes they have made, in the continual reference to the fact the Conservatives party won the last election. We are prepared to admit the great victory of the Conservative party at the last election. We have done so, and I believe that hon. members have received the merited congratulations. We know also we must respect the will of the Canadian people, and their will was indicated at that time. However, we who were involved know also that there was an approach made to the Canadian people which brought about a result of which the Conservatives, no doubt, had a right to be proud of.
There was a marriage made with the electorate of this country. But we also know that there were great premarital courtships and extremely active ones, courtships loaded with promises. For two years now-and this is the third session-the Conservative party have carried the bride over the threshhold. It is now my conviction that the bride has now put her foot down. Let us bring to memory the Gallup polls which have been made in this country recently. Is it not true, that the great popularity of these people who had achieved such a courtship is waning and they find themselves losing some 20 points over a year and a half-
No; it is not true.
-or 12 per cent the last year only. Those are what the statistics will show in the Gallup poll.
That is not so.

The hon. members would appear to want better evidence than that. May I

The Address-Mr. Godin refer them to the Russell by-election which would indicate what has happened-
What about Hastings-Fron-tenac?

-the electors have spoken. Check the merits of the votes. As I understand it-and I do not have the figures with me-there was a large increase in the Liberal majority in Russell. If my memory serves me correctly, there was a decline of Conservative favours in the riding mentioned by the hon. member. This was a clear mathematical expression of the wishes of the people of this country.
With what subjects should I treat on this occasion, Mr. Speaker? They are many and varied; it would take a long time to discuss some of the matters in the throne speech. My problem is that. I do not feel that I may have time in which to discuss those matters I believe to be of great importance and which I do not find mentioned in the throne speech.
As far as I am concerned, the major problems derive from the administration of the present government and from its responsibilities. Since it is quite late this evening, may I give to the house some impressions which I had the other evening on reading a book. As I was reading this book I was, I must admit, possibly thinking of the problems faced by this government and realizing that we are all here trying to assist each other in trying to find solutions to the many grave problems. I do not necessarily agree or admit that they are absolutely their fault in their totality but in a great measure they are the fault and responsibility of the present government. This book related a remark made by a well-known statesman, namely Sir Winston Churchill and it was made concerning this event.
A few years ago Mr. Churchill had occasion to visit our great Niagara Falls which he had not had occasion to visit in the previous 25 years. As he was visiting the falls his companion and guide asked Mr. Churchill this question, "What do you think of Niagara Falls now?" After giving the falls a careful look Mr. Churchill replied, "As far as I am concerned, the principle of the thing is quite the same".
In my own mind, as I recall the problems of the thirties, some 25 years ago, and the Conservative administration in the Bennett days and compare the problems and the approach of the government of Canada today, I find that the principle is quite the same. As with our great Niagara Falls, there is an awful downfall in connection with many assets in Canada. As with our great Niagara Falls, there is an awful splash appearing in


this country after this downfall and it is the Canadian people who are getting wet.
In the last few months we have seen the cancellation of the Avro contract without any preparation to replace such an industry. We read every day about the uranium situation in our country which is not necessarily the most prosperous one. A very few years ago -some five years ago, as a matter of fact- Canada was at the top of the list in the uranium field.
We see in this country the fall of construction industry which is a good barometer indicating the degree of the prosperity of our country. If anyone cares to read the Hugh MacLean report on building in Canada, he will find that construction in 1959 has gone down 10.4 per cent. It is down $227 million in 1959 alone.
Then we have the splash. We have unemployment in our country. Just a few days ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), in reply to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), said that the applicants alone applying for unemployment insurance-and that figure surely is not the totality of the unemployed in our country, but those people alone who applied for unemployment insurance; and if they apply for unemployment insurance they are certainly unemployed- amounted to 722,000 applicants. That is the splash.
Then we have heard a great deal about the diversion of trade and the trade proposals of the government which have had charge of the affairs in connection with trade and commerce in Canada for the last two years. What do we find in this splash? We find a double deficit of trade. All the newspapers in the country were baffled. The pre-marital promise of the present government was not that. As I recall it, the pre-marital promise was much different.
Then we have added expenditures, the conversion loan which occurred in this country and the promises to fulfil and the splashing result, got the tight money policy and the higher interest rate. This affects my people in Nickel Belt as it does everyone in Canada.
The Conservatives went further. To the Niagara Falls splash they added the mist of confusion and contradiction in the policies of this government. I intend to prove that later on in my speech. They went even further than that. They have included the evaporation which occurs at Niagara Falls. Now they have no policy at all. They have tight money without policy, a fact which was well indicated by the Leader of the Opposition just the other night. If we study those promises made and the attitude of the government today, what do we find?

I was surprised, as undoubtedly were many other members of this house, when on the opening night in this debate the Prime Minister of this country had occasion to address this House of Commons during the throne speech debate. I may recall some of the remarks. They were repeated tonight by his parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Martineau). Someone had occasion to state that the art of politics was to make a platitude sound like a pronouncement. If that is the case, if someone did give this definition which I would call a clever one, he was undoubtedly thinking of the administration of the present government. And I would like to prove it. The hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) talks of platitudes. There is a well known phrase coined in this House of Commons, the platitude that "no one person will suffer from unemployment as long as I am Prime Minister". I dare Conservative members in this house to stand up and indicate to us that this is not a platitude.
Then the government says, "If platitudes are not enough, then we will use double-talk"; and how much double-talk is expressed here on behalf of the Canadian people-
The hon. member was doing all right just now.

-in the face of the unemployment in the country, and in the face of the statement I have read? There was nothing novel about it; it was repeated in this house time and time again.
Then there is the reference to the Canadian people who were overtaxed $120 a year under the Liberal regime. What did this government do to the Canadian people today? They kept on robbing the Canadian people of that $120 a year, and $350 million more was added in this country last year. That is an act of this government. The sum of $350 million was added to the taxes of the Canadian people.
Then we have this tax on cigarettes.
That was due to bigger incomes.

I thank the hon. member for his assistance. Here is some more doubletalk, and we remember statements like these. I refer the house to a Canadian Press report in the Montreal Gazette of May 25, 1957, where the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) is quoted as saying:
The Liberals, he said in a 15-minute C.B.C. radio election broadcast, claim that the government cannot increase pensions and increase taxes. "Give us a chance", Mr. Diefenbaker said. "We'll show you".
The Address-Mr. Godin
That is part of the double-talk and here is the confirmation of the double-talk.
Then we have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), who surely must know something about this problem. He should know the problem before the election as well as after, but I would like to refer to something the Minister of Finance said when talking after the election. This illustrates what I mean by double-talk. The Minister of Finance, in his budget speech on April 21, 1959, said on page 2889 of Hansard-this is after the remarks of the Prime Minister to which I have just referred:
We never promised or pretended that these increases in social security could be carried out without somebody paying for them.
Is that not double-talk? Let me add to that another remark of the Minister of Finance. On April 9 of last year, at page 2415 of Hansard, he was talking undoubtedly about the social services intended to be introduced, and he said the following:
The two principal elements of a continuing nature in our increased expenditures in 1958 and in 1959 are the increased old age pensions and the new program of hospital insurance-It seenfs to me that- such universally available benefits should be met from a broadly based system of tax contributions-They cost money and must be paid for.
Is that what was said during the election campaign in a broadcast by the Prime Minister of this country?
Then we have the outlook, not the one which was hidden but the conservative outlook of the people of this country. Up until this time we have had the double-barrelled policy or outlook of economic conditions in this country. That was new enough. We have heard numerous speeches to the effect that there was no recession whatsoever. There were practically no problems in Canada because a certain government had been elected. There were the prophets of doom. Then last session the government said, "We inherited this recession from the Liberals." That was double-barrelled outlook and bad enough, but this year something else has been added. A new vision has appeared of the outlook of economic problems in Canada. It is a sort of three-barrelled policy or outlook. Now this year is the greatest year of prosperity in Canada. Everybody has earned more and spent more, and so on. The Prime Minister, notwithstanding all the problems existing in this country, makes that statement as a new year's policy or outlook for the Canadian people.
Such remarks and policies and double-talk will not begin to cure or remedy the prob-

The Address-Mr. Godin lems which exist. We deplore these problems as much as the government. We deplore them, but we would wish that this government would sit down, as the Leader of the Opposition has had occasion to indicate, and put on foot proper committees to study these problems so that they may be attended to.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock.

speechtext: Are we continuing with this debate tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, we will continue this debate, Mr. Speaker.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Has Mr. Jean-Leon Pouliot ever been in the employ of the Department of Veterans Affairs?
2.	If so, how long was he in the service of the federal government, and in what capacity was he employed?
3.	Has he been retired and, if so, on what date?
4.	What was his salary at the time of his retirement?
5.	On what date did he cease to receive his salary?
Question
6.	On what date will he begin to receive his pension, and what will be the annual amount thereof?
Answer by: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of
Veterans Affairs):
1.	Yes.
2.	17 years 3 months 14 days. Solicitor with the veterans bureau branch of the department in Montreal, P.Q.
3.	Yes, effective 7 March, 1960. At present on a period of four months retiring leave.
4.	$6,780.00 per annum.
5.	Will be paid salary to 6 March, 1960 inclusive.
6.	1 April, 1960, effective from 7 March, 1960. Estimated at approximately $2,372.00 per annum.
